# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.

# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.

It is also a free, on-mission written source, and it is the only place found so far where the ecological-dynamics people write directly about injured people.** Run by **Shawn Myszka and Tyler Yearby** — two of the four practitioners and two of the three textbook authors. [Blog index](https://emergentmvmt.com/emergence-blog/)
215:- **["Part 2 — Opportunities in Clinical Practice"](https://emergentmvmt.com/part-2-opportunities-in-clinical-practice/)** (Aug 2024) — the practical half. Three moves: **accept variability and encourage exploration · keep perception and action coupled · coach to guide problem-solving.** Its best single line for a clinician: **"change the nuanced parameters of a movement problem without changing its global nature"** — that is how you get variability while staying inside pain and tissue-capacity limits, and it is a direct answer to the safety objection Joe will face. Includes a concrete constraint list for loaded work (implement, start height, target height, foot position, grip, time pressure, fatigue, lighting, flooring, social context). Cites Bernstein (1967), Davids et al. (2003), Edelman & Gally (2001), Myszka/Yearby/Davids (2023).
217:- **["Injury and Affordance Perception"](https://emergentmvmt.com/injury-and-affordance-perception/)** (Apr 2023) — by **Javier Miler-Estrada** — **one "l", per the site's own byline and bio, verified 2026-09-02. The Transforming Basketball podcast bills him "Javier Miller-Estrada" with two. Use the Emergence spelling; flag the variant if he is ever contacted.** Co-founder of Ignite Performance (Chandler, AZ). **The closest thing found to a written RTP progression in this tradition**, and it ends in an **ACL case study of a football player** moving from facility work to field sessions against real opponents. Its four moves: progressive contextualisation · **redirect attention off the body part** ("avoid knee valgus" is the wrong cue) · **introduce anxiety and variability deliberately rather than shielding the athlete** · design sport-specific problems ("catch or high-point a ball, then land safely"). **Note the claim that anxiety makes athletes underestimate their own action capabilities** — that is the same mechanism as the Gray paper below.
219:**Also worth reading, not rehab:** **["5 Principles for Effective Ecological Coaching"](https://emergentmvmt.com/5-principles-for-effective-ecological-coaching/)** by **Tyler Yearby** — a course pillar writing the framework in plain language, free. Performer–environment reciprocity · alive movement problems · constraining to afford · repetition without repetition · movement ownership. **Better first reading for Joe than any journal paper in this file, and it is by the lead author of the anchor paper.** Note principle 5's caveat: intervene when a pattern is **non-functional or injury-prone** — the clearest statement of where their approach concedes ground to a clinician.
270:**Recommendation:** take all eight free guides now; buy *How We Learn to Move*; **join the CLA certification waitlist only if Joe's development budget is real** — $1,995 buys direct feedback from the textbook's co-author, which nothing else in this file offers, but the free material plus the Emergence blog covers most of the same ground at zero cost.
317:**Why this matters more than anything else here: it is an injury-driven movement change, solved entirely by a task constraint, with feedback about search direction rather than about performance — and no cue ever mentions the body part.** **That is the entire course in one example. Strong candidate for lesson 0001.**
319:**The two legitimate reasons to change a movement — and the instruction not to fix what isn't broken.** Gray is explicit that you change a solution for **performance or injury** — *"often those go hand in hand"* — and never because it looks unusual: **"if the player is doing the worst ugly swing you've ever seen but their bat speed is high, leave it alone. Don't change things unless there's a good reason."** **In a rehab setting, where "it looks wrong" drives a great deal of intervention, this is the most challenging sentence in the file.** It also names injury as a first-class reason to intervene — **the clinician's mandate, stated by the textbook's co-author.**
321:**What biomechanics is actually for — direct relevance to Eric's force plates and GPS.** The biomechanical finding (insufficient hip-shoulder separation) **was never told to the athlete.** *"This biomechanics is for the coach to design constraints — that's the main thing it's for."* Telling the hitter to rotate his hips more would send him internal. **The data informs the constraint; it does not become the cue.** **That is the governing principle for how Baylor's own data should feed Joe's drill design, and it belongs in the phase-2 tool's design brief.**
339:**Use for:** lesson 0001 (the connection-ball example), the four-goal checklist for auditing any drill Joe designs, the "data informs the constraint, not the cue" rule for the tool, and the evidence list for a skeptical audience.
344:**Source note: quotes below are from YouTube auto-captions, lightly cleaned.** The captions mangle proper nouns (they render Sarama as "Sama" and Myszka as "Shan Mish"), so names here were resolved against verified sources, not the transcript. **Check any quotation against the audio before it appears in a lesson.**
370:**9. The networks connect.** **Shawn Myszka and Tyler Yearby together wrote the skill-acquisition-specialist chapter in Sarama's book.** **The four practitioners in this file and Sarama are one community, not separate camps.**
377:His review of **Sports Coaching Review**'s "Adding texture to the art of constraints-led coaching: a request for more research-informed guidelines" ([doi:10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135)) — **same journal as the Yearby anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`).**
397:**4. He redefines "error", and it changes what Joe should be watching.** Here the athlete never intends a *movement pattern* — they intend an *outcome*. Deviation from textbook form is therefore not an error. His example: Steph Curry's off-balance one-handed three over two defenders in the Olympic final. **No coach would teach that shot. It went in. It was a solution fitted to the constraints, not a mistake.** **Consequence for Joe: score the outcome, not the movement.**
399:**5. Where he concedes the clinician's ground — quote this in a medical meeting.** Gray is explicit that ecological coaches do **not** simply stand back: *"we're guiding self-organization, we're not just standing back and letting athletes do anything."* Solutions must carry certain **invariant properties**, and he names **a movement pattern that might cause injury** as a legitimate reason to intervene. **This is the sentence that makes the approach defensible to a physician**, and it matches Yearby's principle 5 on the Emergence blog.
407:**Use for:** the spine of the drill-design lessons, and **the specification for the phase-2 tool's core loop.** Cite as **expert practitioner commentary** — a podcast, not peer review — but he co-authored Joe's textbook and is reviewing a published paper, which places it well above blog tier.
420:4. **Vaz / Transforming Basketball** — the coaching fix: cue the effect, not the body part. *(Free, above.)*
438:- **Otte, F., Yearby, T., & Myszka, S. (2024).** The Role of Skill Acquisition Specialists Within Sports — Why Every High-performance Sports Organization Needs These Experts! · `key=CKYAA7T6`
460:- **Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., et al. (2025).** The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. *Quest*. [doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759](https://doi.org/10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759) · `key=CA2CRR6Z`
481:- **Lee, M. C. Y., Chow, J. Y., Komar, J., Tan, C. W. K., & Button, C. (2014).** Nonlinear Pedagogy: An Effective Approach to Cater for Individual Differences in Learning a Sports Skill. *PLoS ONE*. [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0104744](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0104744) · `key=XZ8KI5V7`
482:  **Chow and Button are principal figures in this literature, and this is an open-access empirical paper, not a commentary.** **This file is heavy on opinion and light on trials — this is one of the few actual studies in it.** Its subject is individual differences in learning, which is the same argument as the Goes/Araújo coaching study above.
485:  **Harjiv Singh's fourth appearance in this file.** OPTIMAL Theory (Wulf & Lewthwaite) — external focus, autonomy support, enhanced expectancies. **Not the same theory as ecological dynamics, and that is exactly why to teach it:** it is the strongest neighbouring account of the same phenomena, and it slots straight into the attentional-focus thread above. **Joe should know where the two frameworks agree and where they do not.**
503:- **"Micro-Dosing Skill: A Motor Learning Perspective"** — small, frequent skill exposures. Directly applicable to an athlete who cannot yet take a full session.
515:- **Emergence** (Myszka & Yearby) — courses, mentorship, and a practitioner community explicitly built on movement-skill acquisition in football. **Reviewed 2026-09-02: it is also a free written knowledge source, including three posts on the rehab seam and Yearby's own plain-language framework — see the Emergence blog section above.** It also runs the **CSAS** credential, which is a career lever for Joe, and the Adaptable Athlete Podcast.

# Joe's field notes: lessons 0001 and 0002

Returned to Eric 2026-10-20 as a `.docx` (`10-20-2026_Field_Notes.docx`), not in the
shared Google Doc, which is still blank. Transcribed verbatim below, apart from fixing
encoding damage. He named positions only: no athlete names, no named injury.

## Lesson 0001: The drill that hid the deficit

**Date:** 10/09/2026

**The unopposed drill I picked:** A get off drill for a edge rusher. A simple start and
bend drill focusing on lateral loading of the inside foot.

**Line 1. What information was missing from it? What I added:** The information missing
would be reading the o-lineman to determine depth of rush or potential inside counters.
The read on the kick set of the o-lineman is the biggest missing information. I added
myself in there to give a "look" at different sets. This added him having to read the
depth and angle of my set to determine his rush pattern.

**Line 2. What did I see that the unopposed drill could not show?** The on more flat
sets, which required him to take a steeper rush angle he was less likely to get triple
extension rather than at steep sets he was able to run on more of a straight line thus
achieving triple extension. During the opposed drill there were less subjective accounts
of pain or limitation which I attribute to him having to focus on many other things.

**Questions:**
- Is there any sort of prescription recommendation during a session of when to stack the
  opposed / most complex drills? Speaking from the S&C perspective you usually do your
  compound movements at the start, so would this translate to opposed drills in return to
  performance?
- Following that, is there a prescription recommendation about throughout a week how to
  best structure these sessions to meet a "quota" of each drill?
- Does adding zone/man calls or run/pass calls make the drill opposed because you are
  adding information without adding people/equipment?

## Lesson 0002: Attention goes where you point it

**Date:** (left blank)

**Cue count from my recorded session:** Internal 11, External 3, Hybrid 2

**My two most common internal cues, rewritten as external:**
1. When you are about to start take notice to where your collar is compared to your knee
2. Push the belt forward to ensure the belt is not yanking you back

**What I added to one drill so he had something outside himself to deal with:** A pop up
bag

**One line. Where did his eyes go, and did the hesitation change?** Eyes had little
change, and hesitation had little change but subjective complaints went down due to the
volume of other things to concentrate on.

**Compare with my lesson 0001 lines. Did adding an opponent change what I saw both
times?** Yes, but I think with better external cue it will get even better.

**Questions:**
- What are other ways to externally cue without using clothes? I feel like most of my
  cues were coming from what they were wearing instead of their body part.
- Where is the line for cueing too much? When is it best to cue and when is it best to
  not?

# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. 0001 written 2026-09-03 (opposed vs unopposed). |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. `course-map.html` is the 8-lesson plan Joe sees. |
| `reference/gray-infographics/` | Local copies of Rob Gray's free infographics, saved 2026-09-03 because the site is one person's. Includes the 21-study comparative table, extracted and searchable. **Do not republish, do not commit.** See its `README.md`. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** Holds the Myszka book (240 pages, printed 14–253), its OCR text sidecar, the reversible scan manifest, and the extracted bibliography. |
| `scripts/` | `export_for_joe.py` builds the offline package Joe gets on Drive (strips private links; leak check must pass). `velocity_band_sheet.py` builds the Baylor velocity-band sheet (Harries' levels from GPS; writes to Drive only, since it names athletes). Also the book-scan pipeline. `scan_pipeline.py` turns phone photos into a page-ordered OCR'd PDF and **refuses to rename unless the arithmetic gate passes**; `verify_pdf.py` proves page order afterwards by an independent route. Read `scan_pipeline.py`'s docstring before the next scanning job — it carries every trap found so far. |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. 0001 records the lesson-0001 hook decision and Joe's starting floor. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.

# Joe's field notes: lessons 0001 and 0002

Returned to Eric 2026-10-20 as a `.docx` (`10-20-2026_Field_Notes.docx`), not in the
shared Google Doc, which is still blank. Transcribed verbatim below, apart from fixing

## Lesson 0001: The drill that hid the deficit

**Date:** 10/09/2026

**The unopposed drill I picked:** A get off drill for a edge rusher. A simple start and
bend drill focusing on lateral loading of the inside foot.

**Line 1. What information was missing from it? What I added:** The information missing
would be reading the o-lineman to determine depth of rush or potential inside counters.
The read on the kick set of the o-lineman is the biggest missing information. I added
myself in there to give a "look" at different sets. This added him having to read the
depth and angle of my set to determine his rush pattern.

**Line 2. What did I see that the unopposed drill could not show?** The on more flat
sets, which required him to take a steeper rush angle he was less likely to get triple
extension rather than at steep sets he was able to run on more of a straight line thus
achieving triple extension. During the opposed drill there were less subjective accounts
of pain or limitation which I attribute to him having to focus on many other things.

**Questions:**
- Is there any sort of prescription recommendation during a session of when to stack the
  opposed / most complex drills? Speaking from the S&C perspective you usually do your
  compound movements at the start, so would this translate to opposed drills in return to
  performance?
- Following that, is there a prescription recommendation about throughout a week how to
  best structure these sessions to meet a "quota" of each drill?
- Does adding zone/man calls or run/pass calls make the drill opposed because you are
  adding information without adding people/equipment?

## Lesson 0002: Attention goes where you point it

**Date:** (left blank)

**Cue count from my recorded session:** Internal 11, External 3, Hybrid 2

**My two most common internal cues, rewritten as external:**
1. When you are about to start take notice to where your collar is compared to your knee
2. Push the belt forward to ensure the belt is not yanking you back

**What I added to one drill so he had something outside himself to deal with:** A pop up
bag

**One line. Where did his eyes go, and did the hesitation change?** Eyes had little
change, and hesitation had little change but subjective complaints went down due to the
volume of other things to concentrate on.

**Compare with my lesson 0001 lines. Did adding an opponent change what I saw both
times?** Yes, but I think with better external cue it will get even better.

**Questions:**
- What are other ways to externally cue without using clothes? I feel like most of my
  cues were coming from what they were wearing instead of their body part.
- Where is the line for cueing too much? When is it best to cue and when is it best to
  not?
