tools.name: mcp__632f72f2-830f-4b4b-8acd-48153f3c9bed__search_threads
tools.description: Lists email threads from the authenticated user's Gmail account. This tool can filter threads based on a query string and supports pagination. It returns a list of threads, including their IDs, `viewUrl`, and related messages (each with their own `viewUrl`). Each related message contains details like a snippet of the message body, the subject, the sender, the recipients etc. The `view` parameter controls which fields are populated in the related messages. By default (or with `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL`), it includes subject and snippet. Use `THREAD_VIEW_METADATA_ONLY` to exclude subject and snippet. Note that the full message bodies are not returned by this tool; use the 'get_thread' tool with a thread ID to fetch the full message body if needed. Threads with excluded criteria may still appear in the results. This occurs because Gmail identifies matching messages first. For example, if you search for -is:starred, Gmail will find an entire thread if it contains at least one unstarred message, even if other emails in that same conversation are starred. To list threads in a specific inbox category tab, use the `category:` operator with `primary`, `social`, `promotions`, `updates`, or `forums` (e.g. `in:inbox category:promotions`). Note: An empty JSON object `{}` represents zero matching items, not an error.

includeTrash.description: Optional. Include threads from TRASH in the results. Defaults to false.

pageSize.description: Optional. The maximum number of threads to return. If unspecified, defaults to 20. The maximum allowed value is 50.

pageToken.description: Optional. Page token to retrieve a specific page of results in the list. Leave empty to fetch the first page. This is primarily used for pagination to continue fetching results from where the previous `SearchThreads` call left off, especially when the number of threads matching the query exceeds the `page_size` limit.

query.description: Optional. A query string to filter the threads. Natural language queries must be pre-converted into Gmail syntax queries to use this tool. If omitted, all threads (excluding spam and trash by default) are listed. Supported Operators by Category: Sender & Recipient: - `from:` — Sent from a specific person. - `to:` — Sent to a specific person. - `cc:` — Specific people in Cc. - `bcc:` — Specific people in Bcc. - `deliveredto:` — Delivered to a specific address. - `list:` — From a specific mailing list. Time & Date: - `after:YYYY/MM/DD` / `newer:YYYY/MM/DD` — Received after a date. - `before:YYYY/MM/DD` / `older:YYYY/MM/DD` — Received before a date. - `older_than:` — Older than a duration (for example, `1y`, `2d`). - `newer_than:` — Newer than a duration. Content: - `subject:` — Words in the subject line. - `has:` — Has specific content types (attachment, drive, youtube, document). - `filename:` — Attachment with a specific name or type. - `""` — Search for an exact word or phrase. (for example, `"holiday"`, `"holiday vacation"`). Note: Double quotes enforce strict contiguous phrase matching. For topic, discussion, or keyword queries, prefer unquoted keywords (e.g. `partner advertising` instead of `"partner advertising"`). - `+` — Match a word exactly. (for example, `+holiday`, `+unicorn`) - `rfc822msgid:` — Specific message ID header. - `AROUND ` — Find words near each other (for example, `holiday AROUND 10 vacation`). Labels & Categories: - `label:` — Under a specific label, matched by its display name (the `name` from `list_labels`), for example `label:wins`. Label IDs such as `Label_123` match nothing. Quote a name that contains spaces (`label:"Board Prep"`) or replace its spaces and `/` with `-` (`label:board-prep`). - `category:` — In a category (primary, social, promotions, updates, forums, reservations, purchases). - `in:` — Search in specific labels (archive, snoozed, trash, sent, inbox). For example, `in:trash`, `in:inbox`. Archived and sent messages are included by default; use `-in:archive` and `-in:sent` to exclude them. Drafts are explicitly excluded by default by the tool. Use `in:inbox` to restrict search to the inbox only. - `has:userlabels` — Has any user labels. - `has:nouserlabels` — Does not have any user labels. - `has:*-star` — Specific star colors (if enabled, for example, `has:yellow-star`). - `in:draft` — Search in drafts. -in:draft means exclude drafts from the search results. - `in:sent` — Search in sent messages. - `in:anywhere` — Search across all folders, including Trash. Emails that are spam, confidential, encrypted, or suspicious are still filtered out for security. Status: - `is:` — Search by status (important, starred, unread, read, muted). Size: - `size:` — Specific size in bytes. - `larger:` / `smaller:` — Larger or smaller than a size (for example, `10M` for 10 MB). Logic & Grouping: - `AND` — Match all criteria (default behavior). - `OR` or `{ }` — Match one or more criteria (for example, `from:amy OR from:david`, `{from:amy from:david}`). - `-` (minus) — Exclude criteria (for example, `-movie`). - `( )` — Group multiple search terms (for example, `subject:(dinner film)`). Examples: - `subject:OneMCP Update` - `from:user@example.com` - `to:user2@example.com AND newer_than:7d` - `project proposal has:attachment` - `is:unread -in:draft` To prevent overly strict queries, favor concise, keyword-based queries over long subject strings or full sentences. Avoid copying overly detailed subjects from the user prompt verbatim, as this often leads to search misses. Instead, extract the most unique keywords (e.g., subject:amazon \"delivery\" OR \"order\" instead of \"amazon order\"). Use boolean operators to broaden your search coverage. Use OR to search for synonyms or multiple potential senders, and use ( ) for grouping criteria. Note that whitespace between terms acts as an implicit AND.

view.description: Optional. Controls the fields populated for threads in the thread list. Defaults to `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL`. `THREAD_VIEW_MINIMAL` returns `id`, `snippet`, `subject`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`. `THREAD_VIEW_METADATA_ONLY` returns `id`, `sender`, `to_recipients`, `cc_recipients`, `bcc_recipients`, `date`, `label_ids`.

A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

objective.description: The user's underlying goal for this call, in one sentence: what they are ultimately trying to accomplish, not a restatement of the URL or query. Reuse it across related calls. Avoid sensitive information.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. Authenticated searches always add alexandria to the sources, so sources: ["web"] also returns providers; domainTools: false turns off website-matched tools only. enterprise zdr or anon searches do not add it. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

objective.description: The user's underlying goal for this call, in one sentence: what they are ultimately trying to accomplish, not a restatement of the URL or query. Reuse it across related calls. Avoid sensitive information.

tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

content.content:
---
name: teach
description: Teach the user a new skill or concept, within this workspace.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "What would you like to learn about?"
---

The user has asked you to teach them something. This is a stateful request - they intend to learn the topic over multiple sessions.

## Teaching Workspace

Treat the current directory as a teaching workspace. Workspace paths (`./lessons/` and the rest) resolve from the directory `/teach` was run in; only the `*-FORMAT.md` links resolve from this skill's folder. The state of their learning is captured in this directory in several files:

- `MISSION.md`: A document capturing the _reason_ the user is interested in the topic. This should be used to ground all teaching. Use the format in [MISSION-FORMAT.md](./MISSION-FORMAT.md).
- `./reference/*.html`: A directory of reference materials. These are the compressed learnings from the lessons - cheat sheets, reference algorithms, syntax, yoga poses, glossaries. They are the raw units of learning. They should be beautiful documents which print out well, and are designed for quick reference.
- `RESOURCES.md`: A list of resources which can be explored to ground your teaching in contextual knowledge, or to acquire knowledge and wisdom. Use the format in [RESOURCES-FORMAT.md](./RESOURCES-FORMAT.md).
- `./learning-records/*.md`: A directory of learning records, which capture what the user has learned. These are loosely equivalent to architectural decision records in software development - they capture non-obvious lessons and key insights that may need to be revised later, or drive future sessions. These should be used to calculate the zone of proximal development. They are titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.md`, where the number increments each time. Use the format in [LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md](./LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md).
- `./lessons/*.html`: A directory of lessons. A **lesson** is a single, self-contained HTML output that teaches one tightly-scoped thing tied to the mission. This is the primary unit of teaching in this workspace.
- `./assets/*`: Reusable **components** shared across lessons. See [Assets](#assets).
- `NOTES.md`: A scratchpad for you to jot down user preferences, or working notes.

## Philosophy

To learn at a deep level, the user needs three things:

- **Knowledge**, captured from high-quality, high-trust resources
- **Skills**, acquired through highly-relevant interactive lessons devised by you, based on the knowledge
- **Wisdom**, which comes from interacting with other learners and practitioners

Before the `RESOURCES.md` is well-populated, your focus should be to find high-quality resources which will help the user acquire knowledge. Never trust your parametric knowledge.

Some topics may require more skills than knowledge. Learning more about theoretical physics might be more knowledge-based. For yoga, more skills-based.

### Fluency vs Storage Strength

You should be careful to split between two types of learning:

- **Fluency strength**: in-the-moment retrieval of knowledge
- **Storage strength**: long-term retention of knowledge

Fluency can give the user an illusory sense of mastery, but storage strength is the real goal. Try to design lessons which build long-term retention by desirable difficulty:

- Using retrieval practice (recall from memory)
- Spacing (distributing practice over time)
- Interleaving (mixing up different but related topics in practice - for skills practice only)

## Lessons

A lesson is the main thing you produce: the unit in which knowledge and skills reach the user. Each lesson is one self-contained HTML file, saved to `./lessons/` and titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.html` where the number increments each time.

A lesson should be **beautiful**, with clean, readable typography and layout, since the user will return to these later to review. Think Tufte.

The lesson should be short, and completable very quickly. Learners' working memory is very small, and we need to stay within it. But each lesson should give the user a single tangible win that they can build on. It should be directly tied to the mission, and should be in the user's zone of proximal development.

If possible, open the lesson file for the user by running a CLI command.

Each lesson should link via HTML anchors to other lessons and reference documents.

Each lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch. This should be the most high-quality, high-trust resource you found on the topic.

Each lesson should contain a reminder to ask followup questions to the agent. The agent is their teacher, and can assist with anything that's unclear.

## Assets

Lessons are built from reusable **components**, stored in `./assets/`: stylesheets, quiz widgets, simulators, diagram helpers, and anything else a second lesson could reuse.

Reuse is the default, not the exception. Before authoring a lesson, read `./assets/` and build from the components already there. When a lesson needs something new and reusable, write it as a component in `./assets/` and link to it; never inline code a future lesson would duplicate.

A shared stylesheet is the first component every workspace earns: every lesson links it, so the lessons look like one consistent course rather than a pile of one-offs. As the workspace grows, so should the component library.

## The Mission

Every lesson should be tied into the mission - the reason that the user is interested in learning about the topic.

If the user is unclear about the mission, or the `MISSION.md` is not populated, your first job should be to question the user on why they want to learn this.

Failing to understand the mission will mean knowledge acquisition is not grounded in real-world goals. Lessons will feel too abstract. You will have no way of judging what the user should do next.

Missions may change as the user develops more skills and knowledge. This is normal - make sure to update the `MISSION.md` and add a learning record to capture the change. Confirm with the user before changing the mission.

## Zone Of Proximal Development

Each lesson, the user should always feel as if they are being challenged 'just enough'.

The user may specify an exact thing they want to learn. If they don't, figure out their zone of proximal development by:

- Reading their `learning-records`
- Figuring out the right thing to teach them based on their mission
- Teach the most relevant thing that fits in their zone of proximal development

## Knowledge

Lessons should be designed around a skill the user is going to learn. The knowledge in the lesson should be only what's required to acquire that skill. You teach the knowledge first, then get the user to practice the skills via an interactive feedback loop.

Knowledge should first be gathered from trusted resources. Use `RESOURCES.md` to keep track of them. Lessons should be littered with citations - links to external resources to back up any claim made. This increases the trustworthiness of the lesson.

For acquiring knowledge, difficulty is the enemy. It eats working memory you need for understanding.

## Skills

If knowledge is all about acquisition, skills are about durability and flexibility. Make the knowledge stick.

For skill acquisition, difficulty is the tool. Effortful retrieval is what builds storage strength. Skills should be taught through interactive lessons. There are several tools at your disposal:

- Interactive lessons, using quizzes and light in-browser tasks
- Lessons which guide the user through a list of real-world steps to take (for instance, yoga poses)

Each of these should be based on a **feedback loop**, where the user receives feedback on their performance. This feedback loop should be as tight as possible, giving feedback immediately - and ideally automatically.

For quizzes, each answer should be exactly the same number of words (and characters, if possible). Vary which position holds the correct answer across questions. Don't give the user any clues about the answer through formatting or order.

## Acquiring Wisdom

Wisdom comes from true real-world interaction - testing your skills outside the learning environment.

When the user asks a question that appears to require wisdom, your default posture should be to attempt to answer - but to ultimately delegate to a **community**.

A community is a place (online or offline) where the user can test their skills in the real world. This might be a forum, a subreddit, a real-world class (budget permitting) or a local interest group.

You should attempt to find high-reputation communities the user can join. If the user expresses a preference that they don't want to join a community, respect it.

## Reference Documents

While creating lessons, you should also create reference documents. Lessons can reference these documents - they are useful for tracking raw units of knowledge useful across lessons.

Lessons will rarely be revisited later - reference documents will be. They should be the compressed essence of the lesson, in a format designed for quick reference.

Some learning topics lend themselves to reference:

- Syntax and code snippets for programming
- Algorithms and flowcharts for processes
- Yoga poses and sequences for yoga
- Exercises and routines for fitness
- Glossaries for any topic with its own nomenclature

Glossaries, in particular, are an essential reference. Once one is created, it should be adhered to in every lesson.

## `NOTES.md`

The user will sometimes express preferences of how they want to be taught, or things you should keep in mind. This is the place to record those preferences, so you can refer back to them when designing lessons or working with the user.
====
# Learning Record Format

Learning records live in `./learning-records/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc. Create the directory lazily: only when the first record is written.

They are the teaching equivalent of ADRs: they capture non-obvious lessons, key insights, and stated prior knowledge that will steer future sessions. They are used to calculate the zone of proximal development.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of what was learned or established}

{1-3 sentences: what was learned (or what prior knowledge was established), and why it matters for future sessions.}
```

That is the whole format. A learning record can be a single paragraph. The value is recording _that_ this is now known and _why_ it changes what to teach next, not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most records won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`active | superseded by LR-NNNN`): useful when an earlier understanding turns out to be wrong and is replaced.
- **Evidence**: how the user demonstrated the understanding (a question answered, an exercise completed, prior experience cited). Useful when the claim might be revisited.
- **Implications**: what this unlocks or rules out for future sessions. Worth recording when non-obvious.

## Numbering

Scan `./learning-records/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to write a learning record

Write one when any of these is true:

1. **The user demonstrated genuine understanding of something non-trivial**: not just exposure, but evidence they can use the concept correctly. This sets a new floor for what to teach next.
2. **The user disclosed prior knowledge**: "I already know X." Record it so future sessions don't re-teach it. Also record the _depth_ claimed.
3. **A misconception was corrected**: the user previously believed something wrong and now sees why. These are high-value: they predict future stumbling blocks for related topics.
4. **The mission shifted in response to learning**: the user discovered they cared about something different than they thought. Cross-link to [[MISSION.md]] and update it.

### What does _not_ qualify

- Material that was merely covered. Coverage is not learning. Wait for evidence.
- Anything already captured tersely in [[GLOSSARY.md]] as a term definition. Don't duplicate.
- Session-by-session activity logs. Learning records are not a journal: they are decision-grade insights.

## Supersession

When a later record contradicts an earlier one (the user's understanding deepened or corrected), mark the old record `Status: superseded by LR-NNNN` rather than deleting it. The history of how understanding evolved is itself useful signal.
# GLOSSARY.md Format

`GLOSSARY.md` is the canonical language for this teaching workspace. All explainers, exercises, and learning records should adhere to its terminology. Building it is itself part of learning: compressing a concept into a tight definition is evidence the user understands it.

## Structure

```md
# {Topic} Glossary

{One or two sentence description of the topic this glossary covers.}

## Terms

**Hypertrophy**:
Muscle growth driven by mechanical tension and metabolic stress over repeated training sessions.
_Avoid_: Bulking, getting big

**Progressive overload**:
Systematically increasing the demand on a muscle over time, via load, volume, or intensity.
_Avoid_: Pushing harder, levelling up

**RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion)**:
A 1–10 self-rating of how hard a set felt, where 10 is failure and 8 means two reps left in the tank.
_Avoid_: Effort score, intensity rating
```

## Rules

- **Add a term only when the user understands it.** The glossary is a record of compressed knowledge, not a dictionary the user reads to learn. If the user has just been introduced to a concept, wait until they can use it correctly before promoting it here.
- **Be opinionated.** When several words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the rest as aliases to avoid. This is how language compresses.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences. Define what the term IS, not what it does or how to do it.
- **Use the glossary's own terms inside definitions.** Once a term is in the glossary, prefer it everywhere, including inside other definitions. This is what makes complex terms easier to grasp later.
- **Group under subheadings** when natural clusters emerge (e.g. `## Anatomy`, `## Programming`). A flat list is fine when terms cohere.
- **Flag ambiguities explicitly.** If a term is used loosely in the wider field, note the resolution: "In this workspace, 'set' always means a working set; warm-ups are tracked separately."
- **Revise as understanding deepens.** A definition the user wrote in week one may be wrong by week six. Update in place; do not leave stale entries.

1. The athlete who tests fine and plays wrong

37 38

You know this athlete. The strength numbers are back. He has hit his running targets. He is cleared. And in team drills he is a half-step late, he hesitates before the plant, and he does not look like himself. The physical tests say he is ready. Your eyes say he is not. That is exactly the subjective call you told us you struggle to defend.

39 40

There is a peer-reviewed study of this athlete. Rob Gray (2015) tested experienced baseball players who were recovering from surgery: position players after knee surgery batting in a simulator, and pitchers after elbow surgery. He compared them with healthy expert players and with novices. While they batted or pitched, they also made quick side judgements, about the angle of their leg, the angle of their arm, or the ball leaving the bat. The side judgements show where their attention was.

41 42

The injured batters “had an internal focus of attention localized on the area of the injury,” and they batted “significantly poorer” than the healthy experts. The injured pitchers had a scattered, internal focus “similar to that of novices,” and they also pitched worse.

43 44

47 48

Read the result carefully, because a physician will. This is a comparison between groups, not an experiment that caused injury. It shows that injury goes with an inward, injury-focused attention and with worse performance. Gray’s own title asks it as a question. It is also baseball, not football. What it gives you is a name for what you see: not a strength problem, an attention problem. And an attention problem is a performance problem, which makes it yours to work on.

49 50

2. Why injury pulls attention inward

51 52

Singh, Gokeler and Benjaminse (2021) give the clinical version, after ACL reconstruction. “Loss of function, pain, fear of reinjury, and other psychological factors may cause a shift in focus towards the injured area such as the knee” (p. 1). The patient ends up “excessively focusing on the injured area.”

53 54

Javier Miler-Estrada, a movement coach who works with athletes after rehab, describes what that looks like when the athlete walks in. Many post-knee-injury athletes do their warm-up “with their gaze fixed on the ground, unaware and unable to perceive what is happening around them.” In his observation the cause is often “an overemphasis and hyperfocus on their biomechanics” during rehab, with cues aimed at the knee itself: avoid valgus, avoid excessive flexion. The result can be what he calls “fixed and frozen” movement.

55 56
57 Singh, H., Gokeler, A., & Benjaminse, A. (2021). Effective attentional focus strategies after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A commentary. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy, 16(6). doi:10.26603/001c.29848. Open access. Zotero EYKZD68B. Page numbers are pages of the PDF. A commentary, evidence level 5. 58
59
60 Miler-Estrada, J. (2023, April 30). Injury and affordance perception. Emergence blog. emergentmvmt.com. Practitioner writing, not peer-reviewed. 61
62 63

He adds one more link, citing a lab study: anxiety makes people underestimate what they are able to do (Graydon et al., 2012, as cited in Miler-Estrada, 2023; not yet read here). Put the three sources together and you have a chain you can say out loud:

LinkWhat it saysSource, and how strong

75 76

77 78

81 82

83 84

85 86
    87

  • Just before the rep, give an external cue: “focus on landing with as little noise as possible,” or “pretend you are going to sit on a chair when landing.”
    • 89
90 91

SituationInternal (avoid)External (use)

116 117

Force plates, GPS and video tell you something about the athlete. Use them to decide what drill or constraint to set. This is this course’s rule, adapted from how Rob Gray describes his own coaching; it is not a finding.

125 126

    129
  • Gray (2015) does not show that an internal focus causes reinjury. It shows worse performance, in baseball, compared between groups.
    • 130
  • Singh et al. (2021) is a commentary, not a trial. Its strength is in the practical rules (goal before, external cue at the rep, no hybrids). It draws on the wider external-focus research for the claim that it helps.
    • 131
  • Two schools, one direction. Singh’s paper comes from the external-focus research tradition (Gabriele Wulf’s work): it is about what you say. You do not have to pick one to use both. Know which one you are citing.
    • 132
  • “Gaze on the ground” is a practitioner’s observation, not a measurement. Use it as something to look for, not as proof.
    • 133
134 135

6. The sentence for someone who was not there

143 144

# Yearby et al. 2024 — Ecological practice design in American football

> **Citation**
> Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698

## Why it was promoted

This theory-practice paper translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and a constraints-led approach into two concrete American-football examples spanning professional and high-school players.

## Research question

What might an ecological-dynamics rationale look, feel, and sound like when designing American-football practice tasks?

## Population and context

- Participants: One NFL defensive end in the first case and groups of 5–12 offensive and defensive high-school players, aged 16–18 years, in the second case.
- Sport and level: American football, from high school through the NFL.
- Training or return-to-play context: Offseason movement-skill preparation and practice design; not rehabilitation.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Purposively described applied cases from the lead authors' coaching practice rather than a sampled cohort.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Theory-practice paper with two descriptive case examples; no experimental comparison.
- Exposure or intervention: Representative, learner-centred practice tasks created by manipulating individual, environmental, and task constraints.
- Comparator: Conceptual contrast with decontextualized, coach-centred drills; no concurrent control group.
- Measurements and outcomes: Coaches' observations of movement solutions and athletes' comments; no standardized performance, learning, injury, or retention outcome.
- Analysis: Narrative interpretation through ecological dynamics; no prespecified quantitative analysis.

## Key findings

- The NFL defensive-end task retained a centre, offensive tackle, and quarterback so the defender could couple movement to snap and opponent information instead of rehearsing unopposed technique. [p. 15]
- After the offseason case, the authors observed new pass-rush options, including an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, and hand-chop variations, along with more context-specific adaptation. [p. 18]
- The high-school task progressed from one-versus-one open-space tackling to a co-designed five-versus-three run-pass problem with additional positions and changing spatial constraints. [p. 21]
- Across nearly six months, the authors perceived more efficient problem solving as complexity increased, while athletes reported that the game felt slower and that they felt more relaxed. [p. 22]

## Limitations and applicability

- These are illustrative coaching cases, not controlled evaluations; observed changes cannot establish causality or superiority over other practice methods.
- The paper reports no baseline values, objective outcome measures, retention or transfer tests, comparison group, uncertainty estimates, or adverse-event surveillance.
- The authors acknowledge limited American-football-specific applied research and call for more research across performance levels and coach perspectives. [p. 23]
- Contact, fatigue, anxiety, equipment, space, and player-number manipulations change both learning demands and physical risk; implementation requires progressive loading and appropriate medical and coaching safeguards.
- The NFL single-player and one high-school setting do not establish effectiveness across positions, teams, developmental stages, or competition phases.

## Practitioner interpretation

Treat the two cases as design prompts, not validated recipes. Preserve the information that specifies the target football problem, co-design constraints with players and position coaches, and progress opponent presence, space, numbers, equipment, and contact while monitoring physical exposure. Test transfer in the team's own context with predefined football-relevant outcomes.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Paper aim and case range | p. 2 | purpose |
| Theory-practice design and authors' applied context | p. 4 | method/context |
| NFL representative task design | p. 15 | case method |
| Observed NFL movement strategies | p. 18 | descriptive observation |
| High-school task progression | p. 21 | case method |
| High-school observations and athlete comments | p. 22 | descriptive observation |
| Need for further research | p. 23 | limitation |

## Related knowledge

- None identified during this bounded review.

##### _book.md

# Enhancing Skill in American Football (Myszka, Yearby & Gray) — ingest map

**ISBN 9798298178846. Copyright 2025 by Emergence, LLC** — read off the copyright page,
scanned 2026-09-05. Author-supplied physical copy, photographed page by page. Shawn Myszka
was asked for a digital edition on 2026-09-03 and replied that none could be provided, so
the scan is the only route.

**Print → PDF page offset = 0. PDF page 1 is printed page 1.**
The PDF holds printed pages 1–253. It was rebuilt and verified on 2026-09-10.
Pages 254 onward contain only the blank verso and About the Authors section.
Eric chose not to scan them because they add no course material.

Probe: 253 pages, 248 carrying text, `scanned: false` — the OCR layer is real, so
full-text tier is legitimate. Median OCR confidence 95.1–95.5 across the scanning sessions.

**Page order was verified five independent ways.** The fifth is the strongest and arrived
last: the **printed contents page** (p5), scanned after the ingest, lists every chapter's
start page. **All thirteen landmarks match what was derived from the scans alone** —
chapters at 15, 37, 63, 77, 111, 133, 181, 195, 209, 221; Preface 7; Glossary 233;
References 237; Appendix 249. Zero discrepancies.

**Quotation warning.** The text carries systematic OCR noise, notably r→t substitutions
(`structute`, `cote` for core, `playet's`, `emetges`) and `¢` standing in for both `•`
and `é`. **Check any direct quotation against the page image before it leaves the vault.**
Printed pages 155–156 are diagram pages whose OCR text is unreliable. Printed 62, 194 and
236 are genuinely blank.

##### framework--newell-interacting-constraints.md

# Newell's Model of Interacting Constraints

**What it is** — Karl Newell's (1986) model, the operational heart of the constraints-led approach. Coordination solutions **emerge** under three interacting classes of constraint:

- **Individual (organismic)** — the performer: height, limb length, strength, fatigue, injury status, movement history, intentions, emotional state.
- **Task** — the problem as set: the goal, the rules, the equipment, the space, the number of players, the time available.
- **Environmental** — the surrounding conditions: surface, weather, light, noise, social and cultural context.

**The word means the opposite of what it means in ordinary speech.** In everyday language a constraint is a restriction. In this science, **a constraint is a link — physical or informational — that facilitates, limits, or shapes how a system reorganises over time.** Constraints are not obstacles to be removed; they are the sources of information that shape what emerges. This is the most common point of confusion when the idea is introduced to coaches, and it is worth correcting explicitly every time.

**Why it works** — Because behaviour is emergent rather than prescribed, the practical lever is not the movement but the conditions under which the movement organises itself. A coach cannot install a solution; a coach can change a constraint and let a different solution become the easy one. That is why the CLA is a *design* discipline rather than an instruction discipline.

**When to apply** — Any time you want to change what a player does without telling them what to do. It is also the best available audit grid for an existing practice activity: name the individual, task, and environmental constraints currently in play, then ask which one you would move to make a different solution likely.

**When NOT to apply** — The three classes overlap and the boundaries are argued over — fatigue is an individual constraint that a task constraint produces; a rule is a task constraint that carries social meaning. Do not spend time policing the taxonomy; its value is as a checklist for *what you could change*, not as an ontology. And manipulating a constraint is not automatically good practice: a constraint that produces a solution which does not exist in the game has designed in the wrong thing. Pair with [[principle--representative-design]].

**Example** — A receiver keeps rounding off breaks. Rather than cueing hip position (prescription), narrow the space (task), add a defender at a fixed leverage (task), or run it on a wet surface (environmental) — and let a sharper break become the solution that works.

**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output]]: tension - Harries/Supertraining's "concrete" verbal-cue instruction type is the prescriptive approach Newell's constraints-based model argues against
##### framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes.md

# Nonlinear Pedagogy, and What Sits Inside Each Constraint Class

**What it is** — **Nonlinear pedagogy (NLP)** is the teaching framework built on ecological dynamics (Chow et al., 2016). The athlete sits at the centre and **exploratory learning is prioritised**. Its four principles, which are meant to be used together rather than chosen between:

- **Representative learning design** ([[framework--representative-learning-design-audit]])
- **Task simplification** ([[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]])
- **Functional variability** ([[principle--functional-variability]])
- **Manipulation of constraints** — realised as the CLA

The chapter also unpacks Newell's three classes ([[framework--newell-interacting-constraints]]) in more usable detail (Handford et al., 1997; Davids et al., 2008):

**Performer constraints** are **physical** (height, weight, genetic makeup, anthropometrics) *and* **functional** (psychological characteristics — cognitions, emotions). Both shape emergent behaviour, and critically they **vary between and within each individual across different timescales** of learning and development. The illustration: a backup rookie quarterback's emotions entering with two minutes left, down a touchdown. That is a performer constraint, and it is not on any testing sheet.

**Environmental constraints** are **physical** (temperature, wind, altitude, lighting) *and* **sociocultural** (family networks, friends, societal expectations and values, cultural norms). The physical ones are obvious to anyone who has travelled a southeastern team to altitude, or a southern team north in winter. The sociocultural ones are the underrated half: the values and expectations in a state with strong high-school football tradition shape how athletes approach the game and even their **form of life** ([[principle--form-of-life]]).

**Task constraints** are the class **coaches have the most control over** and can meaningfully manipulate: rules, workspace area, equipment, number of players.

**Why it works** — Naming the sub-categories stops the model being used shallowly. Most practitioners reach for physical performer constraints and task constraints and never consider emotional or sociocultural ones — which is why a player's behaviour on a given day so often looks inexplicable from the sheet.

**When to apply** — Session planning and scheduling, not just activity design. Environmental constraints should shape *when and where* you practise, not only what happens once you are there.

**When NOT to apply** — Sociocultural constraints are real but slow-moving and largely outside a coach's control; naming one is not the same as being able to manipulate it. The categories also blur — a rookie's nerves are a performer constraint produced by a task and social context — so use the classes to prompt breadth of consideration, not to file things correctly.

**Example** — Ball pressure and surface wear are equipment constraints hiding in plain sight: balls inflated to different levels, or with contrasting texture, heighten a player's sensitivity to how it feels to throw, catch or carry. No new drill, no new time.

##### heuristic--constrain-to-afford.md

# Constrain to Afford

**What it is** — Renshaw et al.'s (2019) design heuristic, and the operating instruction that Chapters 2 and 3 build toward. **Design problems that invite the player to explore organising more functional solutions — specifically aimed at the opportunities and gaps in that player's skill set.** You do not add a constraint to restrict; you add it to *make an opportunity available* that was not there before.

The book's three design requirements for the practice activities that result:

- The movement problems that emerge should have a disposition that **looks, feels, acts, and unfolds similarly** to the competitive environment.
- The potential **specifying information sources should always be present** wherever possible, so players can couple to them — and the coach can guide perceptual search, educating attention.
- As complexity is scaled and layers are added, examine the **landscape of affordances** the task makes available, so it invites players to perceive and accept a **wider range** of opportunities on game day.

On repetitions the authors are pragmatic rather than purist: accumulating reps **is still a viable way to lead a player into learning** — the priority is on the *nature* of those reps, taken across a wide variety of problematic dispositions. The mechanism of improvement is stated crisply: help the player **change the information they use to control their actions**, shifting from less useful to more useful specifying variables.

**Why it works** — Because skill gaps are usually exposure gaps. A player who has never faced a problem has had no chance to become attuned to the information it presents. Constraining to afford is how you manufacture that exposure deliberately rather than waiting for it to occur.

**When to apply** — Whenever analysis has identified a specific gap. The sequence is: find the problem the player cannot yet solve → design a task that reliably produces that problem → vary it so the solving repeats without the solution repeating. See [[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]] for a full worked instance.

For return to play the audit question is direct: **which problems will this athlete face on their first game back, and how many representative exposures to each have they actually had?**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is a design principle with a strong rationale and a single illustrative case, not an intervention with a controlled trial behind it. Two cautions. First, a constraint that produces a solution not present in the game has designed in the wrong thing — constrain to afford *what the game affords*. Second, in rehabilitation the tissue is a real constraint, and inviting a solution the athlete cannot yet safely produce is the failure mode of this heuristic, not an aggressive application of it.

**Example** — A player who never gets 1v1 open-field tackling reps in team practice will not develop the attunement it requires, no matter how much tackling circuit work he does. The fix is not more tackling; it is a task that reliably generates *that* problem.
##### principle--external-focus-of-attention.md

# External Focus of Attention Beats Internal

**What it is** — Coaching cues fall into two categories (Wulf et al., 1998). An **internal focus** cue directs attention inward, to the movement or position of the body: "bend your knees more," "snap your wrist," "hit it with the inside of your foot." An **external focus** cue directs attention outward, to the effect the movement has on the environment or to something in it: where the ball goes, the position of the safety, the ground being pushed away. From 1998 to 2021 the literature accumulated **73 studies (1,824 participants) showing superior *performance* under external focus, and 40 studies (1,274 participants) showing better *learning*** (Chua et al., 2021). The benefits are durable — still present in retention tests 24 hours later — and they transfer to untrained tasks.

**Why it works** — Attending to your own body interferes with the self-organising control that produces the movement; attending to the outcome lets it organise itself around the goal. Porter et al. (2010) is the clean demonstration: participants ran an L-shaped cone course. Internal instructions ("focus on moving your legs as rapidly as possible", "plant your foot as firmly as possible") versus external ("focus on running toward the cone as rapidly as possible", "push off the ground as forcefully as possible"). Same task, near-identical wording — **350 ms faster under external focus.** Post-trial questioning confirmed the mechanism: body-referring instructions produced an internal focus on 76% of trials; environment-referring instructions, on 2%.

**When to apply** — Every cue, every session. It is the cheapest available upgrade to coaching practice: no equipment, no schedule change, only different words. It is also the easiest first change to sell to a sceptical coach, because it does not ask them to give up any drill.

**When NOT to apply** — Genuine exceptions exist. Where the body position *is* the outcome — a judged sport, or a clinician cueing a movement away from a healing tissue — an internal reference may be unavoidable, and rehabilitation legitimately uses internal cues to protect structures. The effect is also a group average and somewhat smaller in highly skilled performers. And note this is about *focus*, not about whether to cue at all: an external cue is still prescriptive if it names the one acceptable solution.

**Example** — "Keep your knees over your toes when you cut" versus "drive the ground away from the cone." Same intent, and the second is both faster in the moment and better retained. Rewriting a cue sheet along this line costs nothing and changes every rep that follows.

# Newell's Model of Interacting Constraints

**What it is** — Karl Newell's (1986) model, the operational heart of the constraints-led approach. Coordination solutions **emerge** under three interacting classes of constraint:

- **Individual (organismic)** — the performer: height, limb length, strength, fatigue, injury status, movement history, intentions, emotional state.
- **Task** — the problem as set: the goal, the rules, the equipment, the space, the number of players, the time available.
- **Environmental** — the surrounding conditions: surface, weather, light, noise, social and cultural context.
