##### framework--specifying-variables-in-dyadic-problems.md

# The Specifying Variables in 1v1 Evasion Problems

**What it is** — The candidate list of informational variables a player couples to in evasion-invasion situations — the running back versus linebacker dyad and its relatives. Drawn from work in rugby (Passos et al., 2008a, 2011, 2013) and basketball (Esteves et al., 2011), plus Button et al. (2020) and Yearby et al. (2022):

- **Relative angles** between competitors
- **Variations in gaps** between opponents and/or teammates
- **Relative velocity** values between competitors
- **Kinematics, body orientation and postural characteristics** of immediate opponents
- **Any combination** of these

The important negative result: **interpersonal distance alone is typically not sufficient** to coordinate a functional solution, even in these dyadic situations (Passos et al., 2011). Distance is the obvious variable and the one a coach reaches for first, and on its own it does not do the job. The critical values and useful ranges of any of these are **both context- and individual-specific.**

Gibson's compact statement of why the dyad is the right unit: **"Behavior affords behavior."** How two players interact gives rise to the emerging behaviours of each.

**Why it works** — Naming candidate variables converts "read the defender" from a platitude into something coachable. You can direct attention to relative angle or to body orientation; you cannot direct attention to "reading."

**When to apply** — Writing attention cues ([[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]]), and designing tasks that make a particular variable available or salient. Also useful in analysis: when a player consistently mistimes evasion, hypothesise *which* variable they are coupling to and which they are missing.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the authors are explicit about why: **this work is in rugby and basketball, not American football**, and they say directly that research specific to football is needed and that these findings offer "a starting point for applicable hypotheses." Treat the list as hypotheses to test with your own athletes, not as established football variables. Also, because critical values are individual-specific, no threshold from these studies transfers as a number.

**Example** — A defender consistently arrives a step late in space. Rather than more change-of-direction work, test the hypothesis that he is coupling to interpersonal distance alone. Set a task where distance is uninformative — the ball carrier varies velocity without varying distance — and see whether he adapts.
##### principle--specifying-vs-non-specifying-information.md

# Specifying vs Non-Specifying Information

**What it is** — The sharpest and most precise idea in the book, and the mechanism behind several of its other arguments.

Take catching a football. The player must close their hands at the right moment — too early and the ball bounces off, too late and it is not secured. Two players solve it differently:

- **Player 1 uses distance.** They begin closing their hands when the ball is a foot away. This works while the ball is always thrown at the same speed, and **fails the moment speed varies** — which it always does. Distance is a **non-specifying variable** for timing: it does not tell you when the ball will arrive, because arrival depends on speed too.
- **Player 2 uses tau.** Tau is the optical variable specifying time-to-contact. **A tau value of 0.75 always means the ball reaches the hand in 0.75 seconds, whatever its speed or distance.** It is a **specifying variable**, and it works for passes of any speed.

**Why it works — and the claim that should change practice.** Research shows that new learners **commonly latch onto non-specifying information** (Fajen & Devaney, 2006; Jacobs et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2001). And the authors name the culprit: **this is in large part encouraged by the traditional way we practise.** Low-variability, blocked conditions — the ball always thrown at the same speed to the same place — **make the non-specifying variable work**, and so teach the player to rely on it.

That is a stronger indictment than "blocked practice is less effective." It says blocked practice can actively install a strategy that will fail in the game. Becoming proficient means **moving from less useful, non-specifying information to more useful, specifying information** — the **education of attention** (Jacobs & Michaels, 2007), given a concrete, testable meaning here.

**When to apply** — Whenever an athlete performs well in a controlled drill and poorly in the game. That is the signature of a non-specifying variable that the drill made viable. The diagnostic question: **what could they be using here that would stop working if I varied the speed?**

For return to play this reframes the fixed-condition rep. A ball machine at constant speed does not merely fail to build the coupling; it can teach the wrong one.

**When NOT to apply** — Tau is well established for interceptive timing, but do not over-generalise: for most football problems **nobody has identified which variable is specifying** ([[framework--specifying-variables-in-dyadic-problems]] lists candidates, from other sports, explicitly as hypotheses). So you can usually apply the *logic* — vary the conditions so a non-specifying variable cannot survive — without being able to name the right variable. That is fine, and it is the practical form of the idea.

**Example** — The test is one rep. Throw the next ball harder. If the catch falls apart, the player was timing on distance, and no amount of hand-position coaching will fix it.
##### principle--rate-limiters-and-fear.md

# Rate Limiters: Fear Constrains the Solution Space

**What it is** — A **rate limiter** is an individual constraint that limits **the rate at which a performer acquires and develops a skill through exploration of the solution space** (Seifert et al., 2014; Moy et al., 2024). An individual constraint is any physical or psychological characteristic influencing the movement solutions available.

In football, the rate limiters the authors name for young players are **fear of being hit** and **fear of jamming one's fingers when catching.** Both **limit how far the player will explore.**

**Why it works — the affordance account of fear.** Gibson: "the affordances of the environment are what it offers the animal, what it provides or furnishes, **either for good or ill.**" Affordances invite actions with positive outcomes *and* present **opportunities to avoid actions that produce a negative outcome** — failure, pain, injury. Fear is therefore not a psychological add-on sitting outside the perception-action system; it is a **negative attractor inside the landscape of affordances**. The coaching move follows: **modify constraints to reduce the strength of the negative attractor.**

**Ways to reduce it:**
- Play a **non-tackle version** — flag football, two-hand touch.
- **Reduce field size and/or player numbers**, so there is less momentum in the hits.
- **Start activities from positions where information is scaled and intensity is lessened** (see the blocking and tackling activities in Chapter 6).
- **Smaller, softer ball** — directly addresses the jammed-finger fear ([[heuristic--equipment-scaling]]).
- **Change the rules** to remove fear of failure. Moy et al. (2024) is the cited evidence: 40 high-school students played a regulation single-serve volleyball game and a modified **two-serve** game, counterbalanced. In the two-serve game, first serves were **significantly faster, less accurate, and included significantly more jump serves** — the rule change produced exploration of the solution space. The football analogue the authors suggest: **add an extra down**, so young players explore passing, running and receiving without the pressure of a turnover on downs.

**When to apply** — This is the most important entry in the book for return to play, and it deserves to be stated in those terms. **An athlete returning from injury has an acquired rate limiter.** Their apprehension is not a compliance problem or a mindset problem — it is a negative attractor that will measurably shrink how much of the solution space they explore, and therefore how much they relearn. Waiting for confidence to return does nothing. **Reducing the strength of the attractor** — fewer bodies, less space, less momentum, softer equipment, a rule that removes the cost of failure — is a design action you can take this week.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the concept is well-founded and the Moy evidence is real, but it is **volleyball, 40 high-school students, a single acute session** — not football, not injured athletes, and not a learning outcome. The football extrapolations (extra down) are the authors' suggestions, untested. And fear after injury is not identical to a novice's fear of contact: sometimes apprehension is accurate information about tissue that is not ready, and the right response is to respect it, not engineer it away ([[heuristic--right-thing-from-wrong-positions]] draws exactly this line).

**Example** — "He's tentative" is a description. "His fear of re-injury is a rate limiter, so we reduce the momentum in the problem until he explores again" is a plan.
##### heuristic--ecological-questions-and-statements.md

# Ecological Questions and Statements

**What it is** — The chapter's most immediately actionable material: a rewrite table for coaching language. The goal of verbal communication is to help players **navigate the performance landscape** — illuminating information-rich areas and the affordances they specify. Since affordances "do not cause behavior but constrain or control it," asking rather than telling gives the player ownership *and* leaves the solution to them.

**The pattern.** Traditional language names a movement or a rule. Ecological language names **information to look for** or **an outcome to achieve**, and leaves the how open.

| Traditional | Ecological |
|---|---|
| "Why aren't you using the bull rush like we practiced?" | "How can you use the vertical posture and their lack of explosiveness against the OT?" |
| "Stop allowing the WR to eat up yards — use your footwork to stick on the receiver's hip." | "What are you noticing about the receiver's centre of mass height and the sharpness of their cuts when running their route?" |
| "Stop bouncing the ball wide when there is a gap inside. You need to cut back on your 5th step." | "How can you use the LB's speed and angle of pursuit against them?" |
| "You have to drop your hips and get square to make the tackle." | "When tackling, see if you can meet or exceed the level of depth the ball carrier has." |
| "You need to create separation from the DB." | "Show me how you can use tempo changes to create separation on the route." |

**Two failure modes it fixes.** First, **the if-this-then-that rule.** A coach asks a back "Did you see the TE seal the DE?" — then immediately adds "If that happens, you have to bounce it outside!" The rule hinders perceptual exploration, leading players to miss information sources. Second, **the negative instruction that names the body**: "Don't turn your head to look for the ball" versus "When you're covering the receiver, what have you noticed about their eyes and arms as they run deep routes?" — which educates attention toward information that actually specifies ball arrival.

**Timing matters.** General questions early in a session can educate attention to environmental constraints: on a damp afternoon, *"As you move through the movement prep, what do you notice about the way your footing is impacted as you make cuts?"*

**Why it works** — And note the subtle point the authors make: **a verbal answer is not required.** From an ecological perspective the emerging movement solution *is* the answer. The question's job is to direct search, not to elicit a recitation.

**When to apply** — Immediately, everywhere, at zero cost. This is the single cheapest change in the book. Pair with [[framework--direct-learning-attention-intention-calibration]] for the theory of why it works, and [[principle--external-focus-of-attention]] for the evidence.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the table is expert-derived, not trialled, and questioning has its own costs — mid-rep it can add load, and a stream of questions to a player who wants an answer erodes trust. Players must also be told explicitly that **they have room to search in practice and that non-functional solutions will happen** (a back gets corralled while tinkering with speeds); without that permission, questions read as criticism. And where a body position is genuinely being protected, a direct instruction is correct.

**Example** — Take a real cue sheet and rewrite five lines. If a line names a body part or prescribes a sequence, it belongs in the left column.
##### principle--look-to-and-through.md

# Look To and Through

**What it is** — A correction for the most common perceptual fault the authors observe: **players get overly fixated on the most immediate opponent or obstacle in front of them.** The instruction is to look **to** the immediate opponent **and through** to what lies deeper beyond.

Gibson's line is the warrant: **"Perceiving gets wider and finer and longer and richer and fuller as the observer explores the environment."** The authors' shorthand — **wider, longer, and deeper.**

**Why it works** — Because the problem has layers, and the affordance a player should accept often depends on information behind the nearest threat ([[principle--nested-affordances]]). A player reading only the closest defender is solving the local problem in isolation from the global one.

The design consequence is the important half: **you cannot cue this into existence.** The problems presented must *require* looking deeper for the movement to be functionally regulated. Their example: a linebacker moving from behind a defensive lineman, and a safety moving behind the linebacker, against a back navigating a tunnel of traffic between the hashes — roughly 1v3 to 3v3. The layers must be physically present, or "look through" is empty advice.

**When to apply** — Whenever film shows a player consistently beaten by the second defender rather than the first — a tell that attention stopped at the first. Also directly relevant to the [[case-study--saquon-barkley-swot]], whose central weakness was gaze **"anchored too often and too long on the nearest/immediate defender in front of you as if every problem were a 1v1 problem."** That is this fault, named in a real analysis.

For return to play this is a subtle risk. An athlete rebuilt entirely on 1v1 work has been trained, for months, to attend to exactly one opponent — and then returns to a game with layers.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: observed and reasoned, not measured, and the predicted outcomes ("you should notice…") are expectations. There is also a real tension with early-stage work: 1v1 activities are the recommended low-complexity staple ([[principle--low-complexity-activities-as-movement-vitamins]]), and they are precisely the format that cannot teach this. Both are right; the resolution is that layered problems must appear in the diet, not that 1v1 work is wrong.

**Example** — The cheapest fix is a third body. A 1v1 with one extra defender standing ten yards behind changes what the ball carrier must perceive, without changing the load, the space, or the intensity.

Not a strength problem. An attention problem, and so a performance problem: yours to work on.

Two words

TermPoints attention atExample
InternalThe body: a joint, a limb, a movement“Bend your knees when you land.”
ExternalThe effect: ground, ball, target, sound“Land as quietly as you can.”
Hybrid (avoid)An effect plus a body part“Push off your back foot toward the cone.” Say “shoe”.

Three rules

  1. Goal before, cue at the rep. Explain the goal with body words if you need to. Just before the rep, give an external cue (Singh et al., p. 4).
  2. One word often does it. “Movement of the feet” → “movement of the Bosu” (p. 2).
  3. Measurements inform the constraint, never the cue. Force-plate or GPS numbers are for choosing the drill, not for telling the athlete. (This course’s rule.)

Better than a better cue

Put something outside him that he must deal with: a defender at reduced pressure, a ball, a target, a teammate to beat to a spot. The opponent does the cueing. An unopposed drill leaves an anxious athlete one thing to look at: himself. Give him the game in slices, with the pressure down; do not shield him until clearance day.

Football rewrites (this course’s, not the paper’s)

InternalExternalNo cue needed
“Don’t let your knee cave in.”“Push the grass away toward the sideline.”Beat a mirroring DB to the sideline.
“Stay low, bend at the knees.”“Keep your chest under his pads.”Rusher at half speed.
“Drive your knees up.”“Push the ground back behind you.”Chase down a ball carrier.

Eyes down in warm-ups. Hesitation before the plant. Glances at the brace or the knee. A practitioner’s signs, not a measurement: something to check, not proof.

That fits a known pattern after injury: attention goes to the injured part and performance drops even when strength is back (Gray, 2015; Singh et al., 2021). I am not adding load. I am changing [the cue] and [the drill], and I will report what changes over [n reps / sessions].”

content.content:
37:

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

40: Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there. 45:

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 6). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

49:

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

61:

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

69:

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

94:

The course’s anchor paper has the closest case to yours. Yearby, Myszka, Roberts, Woods and Davids (2024) worked with an NFL defensive end in the off-season. Instead of unopposed pass-rush technique, the task kept a centre, an offensive tackle and a quarterback on the field, so the rusher had to couple his movement to the snap and to the tackle’s set (p. 15). Over the off-season they saw new options emerge: an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, hand-chop variations (p. 18). Nobody taught those moves. The opponent did.

97: Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial. 100:

Parry and colleagues do the same for running backs (pp. 11–16). A common “fit off the block” drill, usually run as a script, was rebuilt with a real blocker and a real defender, and then varied by changing who the opponent is, where each player starts, how big the space is, and whether a second defender pursues from depth. The cone drills they contrast it with, they say, “simply do not contain the relevant information that players will utilize” (p. 13).

106:

You said it yourself: you cannot load a lineman at your own size. Parry and colleagues give a ladder for who plays the opponent (p. 15):

135:

Those three questions are this course’s framing, built on Parry et al. They are not a quotation. The paper says a coach can ask “a number of pertinent questions” about a drill (p. 7); these are ours.

content.content:
**Use for:** the individualisation model (rate limiters, PDPs) that the phase-2 tool needs; the "scripted start, live finish" pattern; and the pre-made answers to the safety and buy-in objections. Still **practitioner opinion, not evidence** — but this is a technical interview conducted by an academic, which places it well above his marketing material.

### The single most useful source found so far — Gray's "3 Questions" video

**[A Call for More Clarity on How to Use the CLA: The 3 Questions Paper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0pLFDG-I78)** — Rob Gray, 17 Sep 2024, 47 min. Watched and transcribed in full 2026-09-02. **Source note: quotes below are from YouTube auto-captions, lightly cleaned — check against the audio before quoting in a lesson.**
His review of **Sports Coaching Review**'s "Adding texture to the art of constraints-led coaching: a request for more research-informed guidelines" ([doi:10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21640629.2024.2395135)) — **same journal as the Yearby anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`).**

**Why it outranks everything else here: the paper asks the exact three questions Joe will ask, and Gray answers them operationally.** The critics demand rules for *which constraint, how much, how long*. Gray argues a deterministic recipe is impossible in a complex system — **then gives a usable decision procedure anyway.**

**1. The 70-75% success rule — the operational core, and the drill tool's default logic.**
> *"I let the 70, 75% rule be the guide... if they're achieving that kind of ideal range of success, that's the right challenge level."*

**Above ~75%: add complexity or a constraint. Below ~70%: reduce variability. Inside the band: leave it alone.** **This is the concrete answer to the challenge-point question this file already names as the core problem the phase-2 tool must solve** (see the Harjiv Singh LinkedIn section). **Success rate is the trigger — not time, not rep count, not the clinician's eye.**
*Caveat to teach: this is Gray's practical heuristic from coaching experience, said on a podcast — not a validated threshold. Make it an exposed, editable default in the tool, never a validated cut-point.*

**2. His actual iterative loop — write this straight into the tool:**
1. Choose the **invariant** you want, never the technique. His baseball example: a pitcher's back foot kept leaving the rubber. **He prescribed no foot position** — toe, heel or more knee bend were all acceptable. He wanted only *stay connected to the ground and transfer force.*
2. Add **one** constraint (he used a small ramp under the heel).
3. Give it **at least five or six trials** and watch: **is the movement solution changing at all?**
4. **Changing in the right direction → leave it in** until the new solution stabilises.
5. **Stabilised, or the athlete cannot find a solution → manipulate it** (he varied ramp height).
6. **No effect at all → bin it and design a different constraint.** *"I guarantee you will design a constraint that doesn't work at all. It happens to everyone, me included."*

**3. Variability scales to the individual's success — the progression/regression rule Joe needs.** Same session, same drill: the kid hitting every lay-up gets **more** variability (defenders, new angles, a deliberately bad pass to handle); the kid missing gets **less**. **That is a progression and regression rule built purely from drill design, with no injury framing anywhere in it — the clear

**4. He redefines "error", and it changes what Joe should be watching.** Here the athlete never intends a *movement pattern* — they intend an *outcome*. Deviation from textbook form is therefore not an error. His example: Steph Curry's off-balance one-handed three over two defenders in the Olympic final. **No coach would teach that shot. It went in. It was a solution fitted to the constraints, n

**5. Where he concedes the clinician's ground — quote this in a medical meeting.** Gray is explicit that ecological coaches do **not** simply stand back: *"we're guiding self-organization, we're not just standing back and letting athletes do anything."* Solutions must carry certain **invariant properties**, and he names **a movement pattern that might cause injury** as a legitimate reason to int


# Functional Variability

**What it is** — Variability in human movement is **inherently present** in neurobiological systems (Button et al., 2020; Chow et al., 2016), and it is **beneficial** for solving dynamic problems — which rejects the traditional project of teaching idealised patterns (Chow et al., 2006). Everyone is different and capable of solutions uniquely their own, so coaches should **inject variability into practice to encourage exploratory behaviour** — through purposeful constraint manipulation, or by encouraging athletes to search for different ways of solving the problem.

The word doing the work is **functional**. Variability is assessed by **how practical and useful the solution was in solving the problem** — not by how different it was.

**Why it works** — The chapter's worked example is unusually concrete. A group of defensive backs explore their coverage strategies — backpedal, shuffle (the 50/50 technique), angle breaks, zone and speed turns — against receivers running the routes and tactical situations they will actually see. Following Orth et al. (2017) on creative solutions emerging from exploration, the exploration happens at two levels:

- **The coordination strategy itself** — using a shuffle instead of the backpedal they are accustomed to; using a zone turn where they would normally be instructed to use a speed turn, such as when a receiver attacks their blind spot.
- **The control parameters within a solution** — centre-of-mass height, base-of-support width, speed into the break, length of the penultimate step before planting, amount of body lean, the specific angle of the break.

That second list is the practical gift. It is a menu of things a player can vary *without* changing what they are doing, which makes variability available even inside a tightly constrained situation.

**When to apply** — Any time you want exploration but cannot change the activity — a rehab window, an install period, a positional drill you do not control. The control parameters can be varied within almost anything.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the rejection of idealised patterns is well-argued and the underlying variability literature is solid, but the specific coaching prescription here is illustrative rather than trialled. And **functional is the constraint, not an afterthought** — variation that does not get tested against a real problem is just noise, and a player who explores without feedback from an actual outcome learns nothing about fit. In rehabilitation, the control-parameter list also needs filtering: centre-of-mass height and penultimate step length are exactly the parameters a clinician may be deliberately restricting.

**Example** — A defensive back in a limited return-to-play window cannot yet run every route concept. He can still vary base width, lean, and speed into the break against a single receiver — and find out which combinations actually cover.

Constraints-led return to performance · Lesson 0003

What exactly am I changing?

You changed one thing in your edge-rusher drill and his movement changed with it. This lesson gives you the three words for what you changed, a way to turn each one up or down on purpose, and straight answers to the questions you sent back.

About 35 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.
Built from your field notes on lesson 0001 and lesson 0002. Grounded in MISSION.md. Cheat sheet: reference/0003-three-constraint-classes.

0. From last time, before you read on

Answer from memory.

Lesson 0002 told you to say “back shoe” instead of “back foot.” Why?

1. What you found

Here is your lesson 0001 field task, in your words. You took a start-and-bend drill for an edge rusher and put yourself in front of him as the tackle, showing different kick sets. Then:

“On more flat sets, which required him to take a steeper rush angle, he was less likely to get triple extension, rather than at steep sets he was able to run on more of a straight line, thus achieving triple extension.”

Look at what happened. You did not coach his hips, his feet or his extension. You changed the set you showed him, and his movement changed. That is the constraints-led approach in a single rep. This lesson gives you the words for what you changed, so you can do it on purpose and explain it to someone who was not there.

You also rebuilt, without being told, the case in the course’s anchor paper. Yearby and colleagues (2024) kept a centre, a tackle and a quarterback in an NFL defensive end’s off-season work so that he had to read the snap and the tackle’s set (p. 15). You did the same thing with one body: yours. The paper’s rusher found new moves over the off-season that nobody taught him (p. 18). Your rusher showed you a difference in extension that the unopposed drill had hidden.

Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial.

2. The three classes

The idea comes from Karl Newell (1986), and the course textbook calls it the operational heart of the constraints-led approach. How an athlete moves is not installed by the coach. It emerges from three kinds of constraint acting together (Myszka, Yearby & Gray, ch. 2):

ClassWhat sits in itIn your drill
PerformerPhysical: size, strength, tissue, injury status, fatigue. And functional: emotions, fear, where attention goes.His injury. How fresh he is. Whether he trusts the inside foot.
TaskThe problem as set: the goal, the rules, the space, the equipment, the number of players, the opponent and what the opponent does.Your kick set: its depth and angle. The goal of winning the corner. The distance to the quarterback’s spot.
EnvironmentPhysical: surface, weather, light, noise. And sociocultural: who is watching, team expectations.Turf or grass, wet or dry. Whether his position coach is standing there.

The colours on the rows are the same in every lesson. Lesson 0002’s attention chain was all blue: performer.

The word that trips everyone

In everyday speech a constraint is a restriction. Here it means something that shapes how the movement organises, for better or worse. A constraint is not an obstacle to remove; it is the coach’s lever. The textbook says this is the most common confusion when coaches first meet the idea and that it should be corrected every time (ch. 2). Correct it when you explain this to a position coach.

Three more points from the textbook, and they all matter to you.

  • Task constraints are the ones you control most: rules, space, equipment, number of players (ch. 5). That is why most of your dials will be task dials.
  • The performer class has an invisible half. Most practitioners stop at the physical performer constraints and never consider the emotional ones. That, the authors say, is why a player’s behaviour on a given day can look inexplicable from the testing sheet (ch. 5). Fear and attention are performer constraints. You met them in lesson 0002.
  • Do not police the categories. They overlap. Fatigue is a performer constraint that a task produces. A rookie’s nerves are performer, produced by the task and the crowd. Use the three classes as a checklist of what you could change, not as a filing system (ch. 2 and 5).
Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Gray, R. (2025). Enhancing skill in American football: Revolutionizing practice design for transfer to game day. Emergence, LLC. ISBN 9798298178846. Chapter 2 (pp. 37–62) for Newell’s model; chapter 5 (pp. 111–132) for what sits inside each class. Eric has a paper copy. Newell, K. M. (1986) is cited there; not read here directly.

3. Your drill, as a set of dials

Here is your edge-rusher drill broken into dials. This table is this course’s, built on the textbook’s classes; it is not from the book. Each row is something you can turn down (easier, more predictable) or up (harder, more like the game).

DialTurn it downTurn it up
Your setOne set he knows is comingSteep or flat, mixed, he cannot predict which
What he must readPass set onlyYou show run or pass with your first step (see section 5)
ContactNone, you give groundHands on, then a punch he has to defeat
SpaceWide start, shallow landmarkTight start, quarterback spot at real depth
BodiesYou aloneAdd a tight-end chip, or a back stepping up
StartHe goes when he is readyHe goes on your movement, not a voice
Surface and settingDry turf, nobody watchingGrass, wet, his position coach and teammates there
Him, todayEarly in the session, freshLate in the session, after his conditioning

Notice the last row. You do not set performer constraints directly. You read them: pain, fear, fatigue, trust in the limb. You change them indirectly, through where the drill sits in the session or how much momentum is in the problem.

One dial at a time

Rob Gray’s working loop for using a constraint: add one constraint, give it at least five or six trials, and watch whether the movement is changing at all. If it is changing in the direction you want, leave it in. If nothing changes, take it out and design a different one. He says everyone designs constraints that do nothing, himself included (Gray, “3 Questions” video, 2024; podcast commentary, not a study).

Changing one dial at a time also solves your mission problem. If you turned three dials at once, you cannot say which one changed what you saw. If you turned one, you can: “I changed the set and held everything else, and his extension changed.” That is a sentence an objective person can check.

Is the missing extension a problem?

Your observation has two readings, and you cannot tell them apart from one rep.

  • It is a fit to the problem. A flat set asks for a steeper, bending path. A different push may simply be the right answer to that set. Gray’s position is that deviation from textbook form is not an error in itself: the athlete is chasing an outcome, so score the outcome, not the movement (Gray, “3 Questions,” 2024). Did he win the corner?
  • It is the injury. He may be avoiding the load on the inside foot, the very thing your original drill was built to train. Gray also says a movement pattern that might cause injury is a legitimate reason to step in.

How to tell them apart: compare outcome first (did he win), then compare him with himself. Show him the same sets from both sides, if the position allows it, and set this against any pre-injury film you have. A healthy rusher who loses extension on flat sets and still wins the corner is solving the problem. An injured rusher who loses it and also loses the corner is telling you something. Either way, the form change is a question, not a verdict.

4. The pain reports went down. Be careful with that.

You wrote it twice: in the opposed drill, and with the pop-up bag, he reported less pain and limitation, and you put it down to him having more to focus on. You may be right. That is lesson 0002 working: attention moved off the injury and onto the problem.

But for an athletic trainer it cuts both ways. The textbook is explicit on this point. Fear and apprehension are performer constraints, a rate limiter that shrinks how much the athlete will explore, and you can turn them down by design: less momentum, fewer bodies, softer contact. But it adds that sometimes apprehension is accurate information about tissue that is not ready, and the right response is to respect it, not engineer it away (ch. 9). Pain he stops noticing in the middle of a busy rep has not gone anywhere.

A working rule for now

Fewer complaints during an opposed rep is not evidence that the tissue tolerates the drill. Ask about symptoms after the block, not during it, using the scale your clinic already uses. Ask again the next day, and compare it with a day of unopposed work. Anything that rises goes to Jacob or Tim, the same as it would for any other drill.

This rule is this course’s suggestion, not a finding. Take it to Jacob and Tim before you rely on it: symptom monitoring is their process, and the method has to fit inside it.

5. Your questions

“Do zone/man or run/pass calls make a drill opposed?”

Not quite, and the reason is the most useful idea in this lesson. A call adds a decision, which is a task constraint, and that is a real step up from no decision. But it tells him the answer in a voice, before the rep. In a game he has to find the answer in a body moving in front of him.

The textbook calls this the difference between information that specifies what is about to happen and information that does not. Its warning is that controlled, predictable practice lets an athlete succeed using the wrong information, and so teaches him to rely on it (ch. 9). A shouted “pass!” works in your drill and never happens on Saturday.

The fix costs nothing. Do not call it. Show it. In a game an edge rusher reads run or pass off the tackle. So you show pass with a kick set and run with a step at him, and he has to find which one it is. That is opposed. (This football application is this course’s reasoning on the textbook’s principle. Lesson 5 goes further, with the control-to-chaos continuum and why a coach’s hand signal is still an unopposed cue.)

“What are other ways to cue externally without clothes?” and “Where is the line for cueing too much?”

Your notes caught something real: most of your rewrites pointed at clothing. That is partly this course’s fault. Lesson 0002 gave you Singh’s fix (“shoe,” not “foot”), and you used it exactly as written. Clothing removes the body-part word, but it keeps his attention on himself. The next step is to point further out.

Think of it as a ladder, from inside to out. The ladder is this course’s framing, built on the external-focus evidence summarised in the textbook (ch. 1) and on lesson 0002:

RungPoints atExample for your rusher
1The body“Collar over your knee at the start.”
2His clothing“Collar in front of your knee pad.”
3A target out in the field“Get to the cone at the quarterback’s spot before my second step lands.”
4The opponent“Beat my outside hand to the corner.”
5A question about the opponent“What does my first kick step tell you about where the corner is?”
6Nothing: the drill does itMix steep and flat sets so he has to read you.

Two pieces of evidence for climbing the ladder. In Porter and colleagues (2010), as summarised in the textbook, runners on an L-shaped cone course were about 350 ms faster when told to focus on running toward the cone than when told to focus on moving their legs (ch. 1). That is rung 3 beating rung 1, with near-identical words. Rung 5 is the textbook’s own recommendation: ask about information to look for, rather than telling him a movement. One of its examples is a pass rusher: “How can you use the vertical posture and their lack of explosiveness against the OT?” (ch. 5). It adds that he does not need to answer out loud. The movement is the answer.

For your belt cue, if it is a resisted start: “Push the belt forward” is rung 2. Point past the belt instead: “Get to the cone five yards out before I count two.”

When to say less. The library has no study of how many cues is too many, so here is what the sources do support:

  • Give the goal before the block, body words allowed, and one external cue just before the rep (Singh et al., p. 4; lesson 0002).
  • Questions during a rep add load. Ask between reps, and tell him plainly that failing while he searches is allowed; without that, questions sound like criticism (ch. 5).
  • Where a body position genuinely has to be protected, a direct instruction is the right call, not a failure of method (ch. 1 and 5).
  • This course’s rule of thumb: if you are cueing every rep, change the drill instead. A cue you keep repeating is a constraint you have not built yet.

“When in a session do the opposed drills go?” and “Is there a weekly quota?”

Good questions, and they belong to lesson 6 (how much, and on which day), which uses Taberner’s control-to-chaos work, Harries’ dosing and the Baylor velocity-band sheet. This course does not yet have a source that answers within-session order, so it will not guess. Your weight-room comparison is the right instinct to test: the open question is whether the most demanding perceptual work belongs where you would put the most demanding physical work. Bring your reverse calendar to lesson 6.

The pop-up bag

You found that his eyes and hesitation hardly changed with the bag. That makes sense: a bag does not move, react or show him anything, so there is nothing to read. It is a task constraint with no information in it. That is the question for lesson 0004: does this drill look like his job?

6. The sentence for someone who was not there

Template

“I held [the performer and the environment: same athlete, same session point, same surface] and changed one task constraint: [the set I showed him, from steep to flat]. Over [six] reps at each setting, [he won the corner on four of six steep sets and two of six flat sets, and lost extension on the flat ones]. After the block he reported [symptom score], against [score] on the unopposed day. So next I will [keep the flat sets in at reduced contact] and tell you what changes.”

It names the constraint you changed, what you held, what you counted, what he reported and what happens next. Nothing in it is a feeling.

7. Check yourself

You show a flatter set and the rusher’s angle changes. Which class of constraint did you change?

In the textbook’s terms, what is an athlete’s fear of reinjury?

In the opposed drill he reports less pain than in the unopposed one. What can you conclude?

You want a run/pass read in the drill. Which version makes it opposed?

8. At practice tomorrow

Field task: turn one dial on purpose
  1. Pick one drill you already run. On a card, write its three classes: performer (what is true of him today), task (goal, rules, space, equipment, opponent), environment (surface, weather, who is there).
  2. Choose one task dial and two settings. For example: steep set against flat set, or no contact against hands on. Hold everything else the same.
  3. Five or six reps at each setting. Watch the outcome first (did he win?), then the movement.
  4. Check symptoms after the block, on your clinic’s usual scale, and again the next day. Note it next to a day of unopposed work.
  5. Climb the cue ladder once. Rewrite one of your cues as a target out in the field (rung 3) and one as a question about the opponent (rung 5). Use them between reps only.

Then write three lines: the dial and its two settings; what changed in the outcome and in the movement; what he reported after. Put a date on it. Bring it to lesson 0004.

Primary source for this lesson

Yearby et al. (2024), the NFL defensive-end case. Free full text. Read the case from page 15 to page 18 with your own drill in mind, and list every constraint they kept, changed or added. You will find all three classes.

Also free, 10 minutes: Tyler Yearby, “5 Principles for Effective Ecological Coaching”, the plain-language version by the paper’s lead author. Principle 5 is where the approach concedes ground to clinicians; you will want that line for lesson 8.

If you want the book: chapters 2 and 5 of Eric’s copy of the textbook.

Cheat sheet for this lesson: reference/0003-three-constraint-classes.html. It includes a blank dial card for the field task.

Anything unclear, a drill you cannot break into dials, or a cue that will not climb the ladder? Open this folder and ask. The agent that wrote this lesson is your teacher between sessions and can go back to the sources with you.

The colours on the rows are the same in every lesson. Lesson 0002’s attention chain was all blue: performer.

The word that trips everyone

In everyday speech a constraint is a restriction. Here it means something that shapes how the movement organises, for better or worse. A constraint is not an obstacle to remove; it is the coach’s lever. The textbook says this is the most common confusion when coaches first meet the idea and that it should be corrected every time (ch. 2). Correct it when you explain this to a position coach.

Three more points from the textbook, and they all matter to you.

  • Task constraints are the ones you control most: rules, space, equipment, number of players (ch. 5). That is why most of your dials will be task dials.
  • The performer class has an invisible half. Most practitioners stop at the physical performer constraints and never consider the emotional ones. That, the authors say, is why a player’s behaviour on a given day can look inexplicable from the testing sheet (ch. 5). Fear and attention are performer constraints. You met them in lesson 0002.
  • Do not police the categories. They overlap. Fatigue is a performer constraint that a task produces. A rookie’s nerves are performer, produced by the task and the crowd. Use the three classes as a checklist of what you could change, not as a filing system (ch. 2 and 5).
Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Gray, R. (2025). Enhancing skill in American football: Revolutionizing practice design for transfer to game day. Emergence, LLC. ISBN 9798298178846. Chapter 2 (pp. 37–62) for Newell’s model; chapter 5 (pp. 111–132) for what sits inside each class. Eric has a paper copy. Newell, K. M. (1986) is cited there; not read here directly.

3. Your drill, as a set of dials

Here is your edge-rusher drill broken into dials. This table is this course’s, built on the textbook’s classes; it is not from the book. Each row is something you can turn down (easier, more predictable) or up (harder, more like the game).

DialTurn it downTurn it up
Your setOne set he knows is comingSteep or flat, mixed, he cannot predict which
What he must readPass set onlyYou show run or pass with your first step (see section 5)
ContactNone, you give groundHands on, then a punch he has to defeat
SpaceWide start, shallow landmarkTight start, quarterback spot at real depth
BodiesYou aloneAdd a tight-end chip, or a back stepping up
StartHe goes when he is readyHe goes on your movement, not a voice
Surface and settingDry turf, nobody watchingGrass, wet, his position coach and teammates there
Him, todayEarly in the session, freshLate in the session, after his conditioning

Notice the last row. You do not set performer constraints directly. You read them: pain, fear, fatigue, trust in the limb. You change them indirectly, through where the drill sits in the session or how much momentum is in the problem.

One dial at a time

Rob Gray’s working loop for using a constraint: add one constraint, give it at least five or six trials, and watch whether the movement is changing at all. If it is changing in the direction you want, leave it in. If nothing changes, take it out and design a different one. He says everyone designs constraints that do nothing, himself included (Gray, “3 Questions” video, 2024; podcast commentary, not a study).

Changing one dial at a time also solves your mission problem. If you turned three dials at once, you cannot say which one changed what you saw. If you turned one, you can: “I changed the set and held everything else, and his extension changed.” That is a sentence an objective person can check.

Is the missing extension a problem?

Your observation has two readings, and you cannot tell them apart from one rep.

  • It is a fit to the problem. A flat set asks for a steeper, bending path. A different push may simply be the right answer to that set. Gray’s position is that deviation from textbook form is not an error in itself: the athlete is chasing an outcome, so score the outcome, not the movement (Gray, “3 Questions,” 2024). Did he win the corner?
  • It is the injury. He may be avoiding the load on the inside foot, the very thing your original drill was built to train. Gray also says a movement pattern that might cause injury is a legitimate reason to step in.

How to tell them apart: compare outcome first (did he win), then compare him with himself. Show him the same sets from both sides, if the position allows it, and set this against any pre-injury film you have. A healthy rusher who loses extension on flat sets and still wins the corner is solving the problem. An injured rusher who loses it and also loses the corner is telling you something. Either way, the form change is a question, not a verdict.

4. The pain reports went down. Be careful with that.

You wrote it twice: in the opposed drill, and with the pop-up bag, he reported less pain and limitation, and you put it down to him having more to focus on. You may be right. That is lesson 0002 working: attention moved off the injury and onto the problem.

But for an athletic trainer it cuts both ways. The textbook is explicit on this point. Fear and apprehension are performer constraints, a rate limiter that shrinks how much the athlete will explore, and you can turn them down by design: less momentum, fewer bodies, softer contact. But it adds that sometimes apprehension is accurate information about tissue that is not ready, and the right response is to respect it, not engineer it away (ch. 9). Pain he stops noticing in the middle of a busy rep has not gone anywhere.

A working rule for now

Fewer complaints during an opposed rep is not evidence that the tissue tolerates the drill. Ask about symptoms after the block, not during it, using the scale your clinic already uses. Ask again the next day, and compare it with a day of unopposed work. Anything that rises goes to Jacob or Tim, the same as it would for any other drill.

This rule is this course’s suggestion, not a finding. Take it to Jacob and Tim before you rely on it: symptom monitoring is their process, and the method has to fit inside it.

5. Your questions

“Do zone/man or run/pass calls make a drill opposed?”

Not quite, and the reason is the most useful idea in this lesson. A call adds a decision, which is a task constraint, and that is a real step up from no decision. But it tells him the answer in a voice, before the rep. In a game he has to find the answer in a body moving in front of him.

The textbook calls this the difference between information that specifies what is about to happen and information that does not. Its warning is that controlled, predictable practice lets an athlete succeed using the wrong information, and so teaches him to rely on it (ch. 9). A shouted “pass!” works in your drill and never happens on Saturday.

The fix costs nothing. Do not call it. Show it. In a game an edge rusher reads run or pass off the tackle. So you show pass with a kick set and run with a step at him, and he has to find which one it is. That is opposed. (This football application is this course’s reasoning on the textbook’s principle. Lesson 5 goes further, with the control-to-chaos continuum and why a coach’s hand signal is still an unopposed cue.)

“What are other ways to cue externally without clothes?” and “Where is the line for cueing too much?”

Your notes caught something real: most of your rewrites pointed at clothing. That is partly this course’s fault. Lesson 0002 gave you Singh’s fix (“shoe,” not “foot”), and you used it exactly as written. Clothing removes the body-part word, but it keeps his attention on himself. The next step is to point further out.

Think of it as a ladder, from inside to out. The ladder is this course’s framing, built on the external-focus evidence summarised in the textbook (ch. 1) and on lesson 0002:

RungPoints atExample for your rusher
1The body“Collar over your knee at the start.”
2His clothing“Collar in front of your knee pad.”
3A target out in the field“Get to the cone at the quarterback’s spot before my second step lands.”
4The opponent“Beat my outside hand to the corner.”
5A question about the opponent“What does my first kick step tell you about where the corner is?”
6Nothing: the drill does itMix steep and flat sets so he has to read you.

Two pieces of evidence for climbing the ladder. In Porter and colleagues (2010), as summarised in the textbook, runners on an L-shaped cone course were about 350 ms faster when told to focus on running toward the cone than when told to focus on moving their legs (ch. 1). That is rung 3 beating rung 1, with near-identical words. Rung 5 is the textbook’s own recommendation: ask about information to look for, rather than telling him a movement. One of its examples is a pass rusher: “How can you use the vertical posture and their lack of explosiveness against the OT?” (ch. 5). It adds that he does not need to answer out loud. The movement is the answer.

For your belt cue, if it is a resisted start: “Push the belt forward” is rung 2. Point past the belt instead: “Get to the cone five yards out before I count two.”

When to say less. The library has no study of how many cues is too many, so here is what the sources do support:

  • Give the goal before the block, body words allowed, and one external cue just before the rep (Singh et al., p. 4; lesson 0002).
  • Questions during a rep add load. Ask between reps, and tell him plainly that failing while he searches is allowed; without that, questions sound like criticism (ch. 5).
  • Where a body position genuinely has to be protected, a direct instruction is the right call, not a failure of method (ch. 1 and 5).
  • This course’s rule of thumb: if you are cueing every rep, change the drill instead. A cue you keep repeating is a constraint you have not built yet.

“When in a session do the opposed drills go?” and “Is there a weekly quota?”

Good questions, and they belong to lesson 6 (how much, and on which day), which uses Taberner’s control-to-chaos work, Harries’ dosing and the Baylor velocity-band sheet. This course does not yet have a source that answers within-session order, so it will not guess. Your weight-room comparison is the right instinct to test: the open question is whether the most demanding perceptual work belongs where you would put the most demanding physical work. Bring your reverse calendar to lesson 6.

The pop-up bag

You found that his eyes and hesitation hardly changed with the bag. That makes sense: a bag does not move, react or show him anything, so there is nothing to read. It is a task constraint with no information in it. That is the question for lesson 0004: does this drill look like his job?

6. The sentence for someone who was not there

Template

“I held [the performer and the environment: same athlete, same session point, same surface] and changed one task constraint: [the set I showed him, from steep to flat]. Over [six] reps at each setting, [he won the corner on four of six steep sets and two of six flat sets, and lost extension on the flat ones]. After the block he reported [symptom score], against [score] on the unopposed day. So next I will [keep the flat sets in at reduced contact] and tell you what changes.”

It names the constraint you changed, what you held, what you counted, what he reported and what happens next. Nothing in it is a feeling.

7. Check yourself

You show a flatter set and the rusher’s angle changes. Which class of constraint did you change?

In the textbook’s terms, what is an athlete’s fear of reinjury?

In the opposed drill he reports less pain than in the unopposed one. What can you conclude?

You want a run/pass read in the drill. Which version makes it opposed?

8. At practice tomorrow

Field task: turn one dial on purpose
  1. Pick one drill you already run. On a card, write its three classes: performer (what is true of him today), task (goal, rules, space, equipment, opponent), environment (surface, weather, who is there).
  2. Choose one task dial and two settings. For example: steep set against flat set, or no contact against hands on. Hold everything else the same.
  3. Five or six reps at each setting. Watch the outcome first (did he win?), then the movement.
  4. Check symptoms after the block, on your clinic’s usual scale, and again the next day. Note it next to a day of unopposed work.
  5. Climb the cue ladder once. Rewrite one of your cues as a target out in the field (rung 3) and one as a question about the opponent (rung 5). Use them between reps only.

Then write three lines: the dial and its two settings; what changed in the outcome and in the movement; what he reported after. Put a date on it. Bring it to lesson 0004.

Primary source for this lesson

Yearby et al. (2024), the NFL defensive-end case. Free full text. Read the case from page 15 to page 18 with your own drill in mind, and list every constraint they kept, changed or added. You will find all three classes.

Also free, 10 minutes: Tyler Yearby, “5 Principles for Effective Ecological Coaching”, the plain-language version by the paper’s lead author. Principle 5 is where the approach concedes ground to clinicians; you will want that line for lesson 8.

If you want the book: chapters 2 and 5 of Eric’s copy of the textbook.

Cheat sheet for this lesson: reference/0003-three-constraint-classes.html. It includes a blank dial card for the field task.

Anything unclear, a drill you cannot break into dials, or a cue that will not climb the ladder? Open this folder and ask. The agent that wrote this lesson is your teacher between sessions and can go back to the sources with you.

# Doing the Right Thing From the Wrong Positions

**What it is** — The authors take a phrase heard constantly at coaching conferences — *"being able to do the right thing from the wrong positions"* — and point out that the same presenters then coach athletes to adhere to idealised patterns under a technical model. Their question: **"How can we enable players to do these right things from the wrong positions if we never allow or require them to be in these so-called wrong positions?"**

The answer is **differential learning** (Schöllhorn et al., 2012): require athletes to start from compromising, poor, or simply unfamiliar positions and find ways to do things from there.

**The worked example.** Accelerate from a position foreign to the athlete — an extremely unbalanced stance, low and wide base of support, **leaning opposite the direction they intend to go.** Start every repetition of a set from a position like that, **changing it slightly each rep** — width of base, height of centre of gravity, nature of the stance. Then encourage the player to find **as many ways as possible** to accelerate from each: a transition step, an open step, a crossover step. Repetition without repetition ([[principle--repetition-without-repetition]]).

**Why it works** — Football guarantees bad positions. If they never appear in practice, the only place an athlete searches for solutions from them is in a game, at full speed, with consequences. Exposing them deliberately lets the movement system **search for and discover the affordances still present** in a compromised position.

**When to apply** — Late-stage return to play has an obvious use, and the authors' framing is the useful one: this is not about tolerating bad positions, it is about **having options from them.**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, and the two cautions the authors themselves attach are the most important lines in the entry, so keep them attached:

1. **They are not advocating positions that carry high risk of something bad happening, or tasks inherently dangerous by design.** Unfamiliar is the target; hazardous is not.
2. **Never require a player to execute from a position they feel overly apprehensive about** — for example significant fear or physical discomfort from a previous injury. Some uncertainty from unfamiliarity is expected and fine; **apprehension is a stop signal.**

That second caution is precisely calibrated for rehabilitation, and it is the one most likely to be skipped by someone who reads only the headline. An athlete's apprehension about a position is information about their calibration ([[principle--affordances-point-both-ways]]), not resistance to be coached through. Note also that differential learning as cited here is a real but contested literature, and no evidence is offered for this specific application.

**Example** — Asking a returning athlete to accelerate from a deliberately awkward stance is legitimate. Asking them to accelerate from the position they were injured in, because "they need to face it," is not what this says.

input.content:
Constraints-led return to performance · Reference

The three constraint classes

One page, plus a dial card. The residue of lesson 0003.

The idea

Movement is not installed by the coach. It emerges from three classes of constraint acting together (Newell, 1986, in Myszka, Yearby & Gray, ch. 2). Constraint means something that shapes the movement, not a restriction. Correct that every time you explain it.

ClassWhat sits in itCan you set it?
PerformerPhysical: size, strength, tissue, injury, fatigue. Functional: fear, emotion, attention.No. Read it; change it indirectly.
TaskGoal, rules, space, equipment, number of players, the opponent and what he does.Yes. Your main lever (ch. 5).
EnvironmentPhysical: surface, weather, light, noise. Sociocultural: who is watching, expectations.Partly: where and when you practise.

The classes overlap. Use them as a checklist of what you could change, not a filing system.

Four rules

  1. One dial at a time, five or six reps at each setting, then judge. No change: take it out and design another (Gray, “3 Questions,” 2024; practitioner).
  2. Score the outcome first, then the movement. A form change is a question, not a verdict.
  3. Do not call it, show it. A shouted call adds a decision but gives him the answer. Show run or pass with your body (this course’s rule, from the textbook’s specifying-information principle, ch. 9).
  4. Fewer complaints in a busy rep is not tissue tolerance. Check symptoms after the block and next day, on the clinic’s scale. Never make him work from a position he is overly apprehensive about (ch. 8). (This course’s rule; agree it with Jacob and Tim.)

The cue ladder (this course’s framing)

RungPoints atEdge-rusher example
1Body“Collar over your knee.”
2Clothing“Collar in front of your knee pad.”
3Target in the field“Get to the cone at the QB spot before my second step.”
4Opponent“Beat my outside hand to the corner.”
5Question about the opponent“What does my first kick step tell you?”
6NothingMix the sets so he has to read you.

Questions between reps, not during. Tell him failing while he searches is allowed (ch. 5). Protecting a body position? A direct instruction is correct. Cueing every rep? Change the drill.

The sentence

“I held [performer, environment] and changed one task constraint: [dial, from A to B]. Over [n] reps each, [outcome counts, movement change]. After the block he reported [score], against [score] on the unopposed day. Next I will [change].”

Sources

Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Gray, R. (2025). Enhancing skill in American football. Emergence, LLC. ISBN 9798298178846. Ch. 1 external focus (citing Porter et al., 2010); ch. 2 Newell’s model; ch. 5 classes and ecological questions; ch. 8 the apprehension line; ch. 9 rate limiters, specifying information.
Yearby, T., et al. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. NFL defensive-end case pp. 15–18.
Gray, R. (2024, September 17). A call for more clarity on how to use the CLA: The 3 questions paper [Video]. YouTube. Practitioner commentary.

Dial card

Field task, lesson 0003. Position and injury only, no names.

Date:
Drill:
Performer (what is true of him today):
Task (goal, rules, space, equipment, opponent):
Environment (surface, weather, who is there):
The one dial I turned:
Setting A:
Setting B:
Outcome, A vs B (did he win?):
Movement, A vs B:
Symptoms after the block / next day (vs unopposed day):
Cue at rung 3:
Question at rung 5:

Constraints-led return to performance · Reference

Course map

Where the course is going, lesson by lesson. Each lesson answers one question you will be asked by someone who was not there, and ends in something you can do at practice the next day.

Lessons are written one at a time, after the field task from the last one comes back. The order below is the plan, not a promise: what you find in your field tasks can move a lesson earlier, later, or out. Last revised 2026-09-25.

The arc

See it (1–2)Name it (3–4)Dose it (5–6)Defend it (7–8)

First you learn to see what a drill hides. Then you get the words to name what you are changing. Then you learn to dose a change: how hard, how often, when to progress. Last, you learn to defend it to a physician, a coordinator, or a skeptic with a paper.

Lessons

#The question it answersWhat you will be able to doAnchor sources
1 Why did the drill flatter him? Say why an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, and simplify a drill without deleting the opponent. Parry et al. 2025; Yearby et al. 2024 Built
2 Why does he test fine and play wrong? Spot attention stuck on the injury, rewrite internal cues as external ones, and let an opponent do the cueing. Gray 2015; Singh et al. 2021; Miler-Estrada 2023 Built
3 What exactly am I changing? Name the three constraint classes (performer, task, environment) and turn each one up or down on purpose. Myszka, Yearby & Gray (textbook); Yearby et al. 2024 Planned
4 Does this drill look like his job? State what a position has to read and do, and judge whether a drill samples it. Why a cone drill is not agility. Yearby et al. 2024; Young et al. 2022 (IUSCA agility); textbook Planned
5 When do I make it harder? Use his success rate as the dial for progressing or regressing a drill, and read the control-to-chaos continuum ecologically: why a coach's hand signal is still an unopposed cue. # Joe can simplify without deleting; his cues stop at clothing; lesson 0003 built on his own drill

Joe's field notes for lessons 0001 and 0002 came back on 2026-10-20
(`field-notes/2026-10-20-joe-field-notes-0001-0002.md`). They are the first evidence of
learning in this course, and they set the floor for lesson 0003.

## Evidence

- **Opposed vs unopposed: demonstrated.** For an edge rusher he replaced an unopposed
  start-and-bend drill with himself as the tackle showing varied kick sets. He kept the
  opponent and reduced the pressure, which is simplification, not decomposition. He then
  saw a coupling the unopposed drill hid: flat sets → steeper rush angle → less triple
  extension. Both glossary candidates from record 0001 are promoted to `GLOSSARY.md`.
- **External focus: half-learned, and partly the course's doing.** Cue count 11 internal,
  3 external, 2 hybrid. His rewrites point at clothing ("collar", "belt"). Lesson 0002 gave
  him Singh's "shoe, not foot" fix and he applied it literally. He noticed the limit himself
  and asked for alternatives. He does not yet have targets out in the field or questions
  about the opponent as cue forms.
- **Static objects carry no information.** A pop-up bag changed neither his athlete's eyes
  nor his hesitation. He reported it without yet explaining why: evidence for lesson 0004.
- **A clinical blind spot to watch.** Twice he read fewer in-rep pain complaints under
  higher attentional load as a plain positive.

## Decisions for lesson 0003

- Taught Newell's three classes through Joe's own drill, broken into dials (the dial table
  is the course's). Anchors: textbook ch. 2 and 5 via the library atoms; the Yearby (2024)
  NFL defensive-end case as the primary source, since it is the same drill.
- "One dial at a time, five or six reps" taken from Gray's "3 Questions" video (practitioner,
  auto-caption transcript; paraphrased, not quoted).
- Pain observation handled as a working rule labelled as the course's suggestion, anchored to
  the textbook's rate-limiter idea (ch. 9) and the authors' apprehension line (ch. 8). Joe is
  told to agree it with Jacob and Tim. **Eric should confirm this framing; it was not
  discussed with him before the lesson was built.**
- His questions answered in the lesson: run/pass calls (show it, don't call it, from the
  specifying-information principle, ch. 9; full treatment stays in lesson 5); cueing without
  clothes (the cue ladder, the course's framing on ch. 1 and ch. 5); session order and weekly
  quota deferred to lesson 6 rather than guessed.
- Textbook quotations were paraphrased: the library atoms are not checked against page
  images, and the book PDF is on the Mac only.

## Gaps

- No source in the library on cue frequency, or on near vs far external focus. The lesson
  says so. Acquisition candidate: Chua et al. (2021) review, cited in the textbook ch. 1.
- Within-session ordering of perceptual work has no source yet. Needed before lesson 6.

# Constraints-Led Return to Performance Glossary

The working language of this course: ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach,
applied to return to performance in American football. A term is added only once Joe has
used it correctly in his own field work.

## Terms

**Unopposed practice**:
Practice with no opponent present, so the athlete runs a plan he already knows and has nothing to read.
_Avoid_: Individual work, technique work (when used to mean "evidence of readiness")

**Opposed practice**:
Practice that keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem changes rep to rep and cannot be fully predicted.
_Avoid_: Live work, team work

**Simplify**:
Make a task easier while keeping the information it runs on, for example by reducing the opponent's pressure rather than removing the opponent. Added 2026-10-20 (Joe used himself as a reduced-pressure tackle).
_Avoid_: Regress (when it means stripping the opponent out)

**Decompose**:
Break a task into parts and practise them separately, which removes the information that links them. The opposite move to simplify.
_Avoid_: Break it down, progress from the parts

lines: -# RTP_Constraints_Course
-A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
-(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).
-**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
-**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
-**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
-phase of return to performance in American football.
-## How to work here
-Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
-`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
-slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.
-Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
-wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.
-## Layout
-| Path | What it is |
-| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
-| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |

-| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
-| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
-| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |

Lesson 3 is built, committed and pushed, but Joe doesn't have it yet. I held the export to his Drive folder until you've read section 4, the pain section. The Google Doc isn't filled in yet either.

**What's new in the repo**
- [lessons/0003-what-exactly-am-i-changing.html](RTP_Constraints_Course/lessons/0003-what-exactly-am-i-changing.html), about 35 minutes for Joe.
- [reference/0003-three-constraint-classes.html](RTP_Constraints_Course/reference/0003-three-constraint-classes.html): a cheat sheet that prints on two pages, plus a blank card for his field task on a third.
- Learning record 0003 and the first `GLOSSARY.md`. Joe's notes show he now uses opposed/unopposed and simplify/decompose correctly, so those four terms went in.
- The course map shows lesson 3 as Built; NOTES and STATUS are updated.
- The tests pass, and a trial export passed the check that nothing private leaks out.

**What the lesson covers**
- **His drill is the example.** The three constraint classes (performer, task, environment) are taught through his own edge-rusher drill. His flat-set vs steep-set observation is the opening, and the Yearby defensive-end case from lesson 1 is the primary source.
- **One change at a time.** It shows his drill as a set of dials he can turn up or down. The rule is to change one dial, run five or six reps, then judge. That also gives him a sentence he can defend to someone objective.
- **His questions get direct answers:**
  - Run/pass calls: "don't call it, show it with your first step."
  - Cueing without clothing: a ladder that runs from body, to clothing, to a target out on the field, to the opponent, to a question about the opponent.
  - When to stop cueing: "if you're cueing every rep, change the drill instead."
  - Session order and weekly quotas are honestly deferred to lesson 6.
- **The clothing cues were partly our fault.** Lesson 2 told him to say "shoe" instead of "foot," and he followed it exactly. The lesson says so.

**Section 4 is the part to read before Joe gets it.** It tells him that fewer pain complaints during an opposed rep is not evidence that the tissue can handle the drill. It has him check symptoms after the block and the next day, on the clinic's usual scale, and agree that check with Jacob and Tim. It rests on the textbook authors' own caution: never make a player work from a position he's very apprehensive about. That rule is mine, not a study finding, so you should agree with it before it goes out.

**The Google Doc isn't filled in.** The `gws` command-line tool fails to log in on this laptop. The browser pane is signed in as buckcomandr@gmail.com, which has no access to the doc, and I didn't request access. If you sign in as eric.rash11@gmail.com there, or let me use Claude in Chrome, I can fill it in.

**Two things you should know:**
- `CLAUDE.md` says lessons come only through `/teach`. Since you asked me directly, I built this lesson by hand, following the teach skill's instructions step by step.
- The library has nothing on how often to cue or on near vs far targets for external cues. The lesson says so. I added the Chua et al. (2021) review to the list of sources to get.
